passages: Nvidia's Board of Directors is preparing to oust co-founder and chief executive Jensen Huang following revelations of two extramarital affairs, including one with a woman suspected of working for Chinese intelligence and another with an Nvidia executive , reports The Wall Street Journal .
Although no final decision has been made yet, the company's directors could meet as early as November 11 to discuss Huang's future.
Nvidia's stock dropped 8% in after-hours trading following the reports.

Huang's potential departure would mark the first CEO transition in Nvidia's 33-year history, and therefore his succession has become an immediate concern for Nvidia, which does not have anyone of Huang's caliber in the leadership team.
However, has not served in an executive role at Nvidia for at least a decade, so the chances that he will succeed Huang are low.

The report from the WSJ comes hours after the New York Times revealed that Huang allegedly had an extramarital relationship with Kimberly Powell , Nvidia's vice president of health care, who reports directly to him.
According to five people who worked at Nvidia, the relationship was known internally, while Huang and Powell were reportedly seen together at a San Jose hotel during Nvidia's GTC conference in March.
Anton Shilov is a contributing writer at Tom’s Hardware.
Over the past couple of decades, he has covered everything from CPUs and GPUs to supercomputers and from modern process technologies and latest fab tools to high-tech industry trends.
Back on Sunday, directors expressed confidence in Jensen Huang and his leadership team, a choice of words that did not exactly guarantee his continued tenure.

That came three days after Huang told employees he had been unfaithful to his wife, following reports that linked him to Alice Huang, a former executive at Singapore's Megaspeed whom U.S. officials suspect of spying for China.

The first-day drops were small in both cases, under 3%.

What separated the two outcomes came later, and it was mostly about two things: whether the board had a successor ready on day one, and whether the business underneath was healthy.
Intel had neither, and its stock lagged for the year that followed.
Huang being removed immediately could be challenging for Nvidia since it does not have a succession plan in place," Gil Luria of D.A.
Davidson told Reuters after the Journal's report.
Huang co-founded the company in 1993 and has run it ever since, which makes him harder to replace than Krzanich or Easterbrook, who were both hired managers.
Baird analysts Tristan Gerra and Tyler Bomba wrote earlier Wednesday that a CEO change was growing more likely and that an outside hire would be favored.
Dan Ives of Yorkville Ives has said Nvidia would be worth 25% to 30% less without Huang.
On the other side, Nvidia's business is far healthier than Intel's was in 2018, and a Blind survey found 88% of 232 Nvidia employees want Huang to stay.
For a holder with $100,000 in Nvidia, about 621 shares at the after-hours price, the two histories frame the range.
Neither history includes a founder, so the real range is probably wider in both directions.

In August 2020 the company sued Easterbrook, saying he had hidden other relationships, and in 2021 he agreed to return more than $105 million in pay.

Chief financial officer Bob Swan ran the company as interim CEO for seven months before the board gave him the job in January 2019, while Intel was also struggling to get its next generation of chips into production.
A fast, credible choice was the difference between the two cases above.

Nvidia has not commented. The report came shortly after a New York Times story that Huang had a relationship with Kimberly Powell, Nvidia's vice president of healthcare and one of roughly 60 executives who report to him, citing five former employees. Nvidia was at $160.95 in after-hours trading at 6:30 PM ET, down 7.4% from Wednesday's close and 13.8% from the November 6 close, the last before Huang's admission. A relationship with a direct report turns the board's problem into one that boards have handled before, and twice in the past decade the CEO had to go. Here is what happened to shareholders those two times.

On June 21, 2018, Intel said CEO Brian Krzanich had resigned after an investigation found a past consensual relationship with an employee, which broke a company policy that applied to managers. Intel had no successor ready. Chief financial officer Bob Swan ran the company as interim CEO for seven months before the board gave him the job in January 2019, while Intel was also struggling to get its next generation of chips into production.

Intel stock fell 2.4% that day, counting from the prior close, while the S&P 500 fell 0.6%. A year later, with dividends counted, Intel was down 8.7% while the S&P 500 was up 8.5%, a gap of 17 percentage points.

On Sunday, November 3, 2019, McDonald's said its board had fired CEO Steve Easterbrook for a consensual relationship with an employee, which violated company policy. The board named Chris Kempczinski, who ran the U.S. business, as CEO in the same announcement. In August 2020 the company sued Easterbrook, saying he had hidden other relationships, and in 2021 he agreed to return more than $105 million in pay.

McDonald's stock fell 2.7% the next trading day. A year later, with dividends counted, it was up 14.7%, ahead of the S&P 500's 11.9%, even with the 2020 crash in between. Six months in, during that crash, both McDonald's and the index were down: 7.6% and 6.1%.

The first-day drops were small in both cases, under 3%. Nvidia has already fallen more than that after hours tonight alone. What separated the two outcomes came later, and it was mostly about two things: whether the board had a successor ready on day one, and whether the business underneath was healthy. McDonald's had both. Intel had neither, and its stock lagged for the year that followed.

Nvidia has no named successor. "Mr. Huang being removed immediately could be challenging for Nvidia since it does not have a succession plan in place," Gil Luria of D.A. Davidson told Reuters after the Journal's report. Huang co-founded the company in 1993 and has run it ever since, which makes him harder to replace than Krzanich or Easterbrook, who were both hired managers. Baird analysts Tristan Gerra and Tyler Bomba wrote earlier Wednesday that a CEO change was growing more likely and that an outside hire would be favored. Dan Ives of Yorkville Ives has said Nvidia would be worth 25% to 30% less without Huang. On the other side, Nvidia's business is far healthier than Intel's was in 2018, and a Blind survey found 88% of 232 Nvidia employees want Huang to stay.

For a holder with $100,000 in Nvidia, about 621 shares at the after-hours price, the two histories frame the range. On the Intel path the stake would be worth about $91,334 a year from now; on the McDonald's path, about $114,657. Neither history includes a founder, so the real range is probably wider in both directions.

The useful question for a holder is the one the board will answer first: whether Nvidia names a successor quickly or leaves the job open. A fast, credible choice was the difference between the two cases above. Until that is known, the position size is the decision a holder controls, and a stake that would hurt at the Intel outcome is a stake worth trimming, preferably inside an IRA, where selling does not trigger a tax bill.

Nvidia did not immediately respond to requests for comment about the new reports. Days earlier, Nvidia’s board said it would investigate whether Huang was the “target of a foreign intelligence effort” amid reports that he had a separate relationship with a woman US officials believe to be a Chinese spy. Huang on Sunday apologized for an extramarital affair, although he did not name the other party. Huang is without a clear No. 2 if the board decides to remove him, with the founder having previously said he does not believe in succession planning. “Our company was built so that I know how to run it,” he told Bloomberg in 2023. “So for as long as I’m running it, that’s all that matters.” Investors are weighing the outlook for the chipmaker that’s been at the center of the AI boom if Huang is ousted from his role. The CEO has been one of AI’s most steadfast cheerleaders and funders, and investors have flocked to Nvidia shares because of his vision for the tech boom. Nvidia shares dropped 9.5% across Monday and Tuesday after Huang’s weekend admission of extramarital affair and news of the Nvidia board’s investigation. Shares rebounded Wednesday during trading, rising 2.9%, before tumbling in after-hours trading and erasing those gains. Nvidia shares were down 27% from a peak in early October as of the market close on Wednesday, before the sharp after-hours decline. The drop in Nvidia shares weighed on the broader market: Nasdaq 100 futures fell 1.1% and S&P 500 futures fell 0.5% as of 6:30 p.m ET. While Nvidia shares tumbled, shares of other major semiconductor chipmakers moved higher. Advanced Micro Devices shares ( AMD ) rose 3.75% as of 6 p.m. ET, while Broadcom shares ( AVGO ) rose 2.7%. Nvidia shares dropped 9.5% across Monday and Tuesday after Huang’s weekend admission of extramarital affair and news of the Nvidia board’s investigation. Shares rebounded Wednesday during trading, rising 2.9%, before tumbling in after-hours trading and erasing those gains. Nvidia shares were down 27% from a peak in early October as of the market close on Wednesday, before the sharp after-hours decline. The drop in Nvidia shares weighed on the broader market: Nasdaq 100 futures fell 1.1% and S&P 500 futures fell 0.5% as of 6:30 p.m ET. relevantPassages.text: Jensen Huang, CEO of Nvidia, gives a keynote address on October 21 in Berlin.

(CNN) — Nvidia shares dropped sharply in after-hours trading on Wednesday after reports that CEO Jensen Huang had an extramarital relationship with a company executive and that the board is meeting to discuss his future.
The drop in Nvidia shares weighed on the broader market: Nasdaq 100 futures fell 1.1% and S&P 500 futures fell 0.5% as of 6:30 p.m ET.
Huang on Sunday apologized for an extramarital affair, although he did not name the other party.
Investors are weighing the outlook for the chipmaker that’s been at the center of the AI boom if Huang is ousted from his role.
The CEO has been one of AI’s most steadfast cheerleaders and funders, and investors have flocked to Nvidia shares because of his vision for the tech boom.
Nvidia did not immediately respond to requests for comment about the new reports.

extraction.body: Watch: Who is suspected Chinese spy at centre of Nvidia affair investigation? One of the Artificial Intelligence (AI) industry's most important figures has been accused of having an affair with a suspected Chinese spy. US intelligence officials believed that Chinese businesswoman Alice Huang, who had a close relationship with Nvidia chief executive and co-founder Jensen Huang, was a spy for Beijing , according to a New York Times report. Jensen Huang admitted , external to having been "unfaithful" to his wife and apologised for hurting her and their children. Nvidia, one of the most valuable companies in the world, has opened an independent investigation into the affair. It said it does not believe US national security had been compromised - and added that Jensen Huang is committed to continuing to lead the company. Here is what we know about the affair and why it matters. Jensen Huang (left) and Alice Huang - also known as Huang Le - at an event Alice Huang, no relation to Jensen Huang, was a top executive at Singapore-based data centre firm Megaspeed between March and November 2023. The company had been suspected of helping divert Nvidia chips to China. Nvidia said this was investigated and debunked. However, Megaspeed is under investigation by the Singapore government regarding previous allegations that the company was circumventing US sanctions on the export of Nvidia's high-end chips. Foreign Ministry spokesperson Guo Jiakun said: "The allegations about Chinese spies are entirely groundless, speculative and intended to smear and malign China." There were media reports in October that US President Donald Trump had been briefed last year on intelligence alleging Alice Huang was spying on China's behalf. US Secretary of State Marco Rubio, meanwhile, refused to comment when asked about Jensen Huang. In spring this year, the secretary of state reportedly oversaw the drafting of a memo that warned the Trump administration about Jensen Huang's relationship with the Chinese businesswoman. Trump says FBI investigating Nvidia boss's affair with alleged Chinese spy Zoe Kleinman: Nvidia CEO's affair will cause ripples across US and beyond Nvidia hires major New York law firm to investigate Jensen Huang affair Nvidia is at the heart of US and China's AI race , which is why the billionaire boss's affair has sparked national security fears among American lawmakers. Trump has said "whoever wins AI wins", and the concern is that if China gains the upper hand in AI, it will supercharge the country's military and surveillance capabilities. The US advantage is in large part because of companies like Nvidia, working with producers such as the Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company (TSMC), which makes more than 90% of the world's most advanced chips. Since 2022, the US has used various export controls to keep the top tech out of China, which it says helps retain America's competitive edge and protects its national security. This means companies like Nvidia have been largely locked out of the world's most lucrative market, with Jensen Huang once saying that Nvidia's share of the Chinese market had gone from around 95% to effectively zero. Jensen Huang has engaged in shuttle diplomacy between Washington and Beijing, hoping to find a US-approved way back in, and shaping US policy on China along the way. The revelations may explain why Jensen Huang has failed to bring home the biggest prize of all to Nvidia: the Trump administration's blessing to sell all but its most advanced chips to China . Born in Taiwan in 1963, Jensen Huang was nine years old when his family moved to the West Coast of the US. He graduated as an electrical engineer from Oregon State University, and then with a master's degree in the same field from Stanford University. He worked at US chip firm AMD before co-founding Nvidia. Known as "Daddy Huang" in Taiwan and once lauded as the "Taylor Swift of tech" , he has a reputation as a workaholic with incredibly high standards for his staff. He has an estimated fortune of $155bn (£115bn), according to the Bloomberg Billionaires Index. "Jensen Huang is a tech visionary of the likes of Steve Jobs," Stephen Witt, the author of Thinking Machine, a biography on the Jensen Huang, told the BBC, adding that he was responsible for creating AI hardware as we know it today. The Nvidia co-founder has a famously close relationship with Trump. At the recent AI summit at the White House, where 42 tech executives were present, the president was flanked by Elon Musk and Jensen Huang. Trump said he spoke with Jensen Huang after reports emerged about Alice Huang and her alledged links to the Chinese state and asked him: "'Did you have any idea she was a spy? "He said 'I had no idea she was a spy' and I really believe him," said Trump. Nvidia has launched an independent investigation into the affair and has hired New York law firm Wachtell, Lipton, Rosen & Katz. It will be led by Joon Kim, a former US Attorney for New York's Southern District who is now at litigation partner at the law firm. Jensen Huang has also been asked to appear for a joint closed-door briefing for several Congressional committees on 18 November. Members of the US House Foreign Affairs Committee asked the Nvidia chief executive to appear to explain his interactions with Alice Huang, as well as Nvidia's security protocols around espionage.

extraction.body: Tech executive Alice Huang is the woman accused of spying for China during an affair with Jensen Huang, head of US artificial intelligence chip titan Nvidia, according to media reports. Public details are sparse about the woman, also known as Huang Le, who had reportedly been a top figure at a Singapore-based data centre company called Megaspeed International. Here is what we know about her and the company: Alice Huang is a Chinese citizen recruited by Beijing to collect intelligence on the Nvidia boss, according to the New York Times, which first reported that Jensen Huang was the alleged target of a spy plot. Despite their shared surname, Alice Huang is no relation to the 63-year-old Taiwanese-born head of the world's most valuable company. The Times, citing people briefed on the surveillance, said that Alice Huang speaks good English and is well connected at the highest level of the global AI chip industry. The sector is highly sensitive as the United States and China race to develop advanced AI systems with potential military applications. An online search brought up a short profile for Alice Huang, with her photo, on a Chinese fund database. It listed previous jobs including at HSBC bank, and as a reporter for Chinese media outlets CCTV and Hunan TV. AFP was unable to verify the contents of the profile, or who had written it, but has attempted to contact the companies cited. Media reports last week said they had a close relationship, and Jensen Huang told Nvidia employees on Sunday he was "deeply sorry" for being "unfaithful to my wife". One photo from an industry party in 2024, posted on LinkedIn, appears to show the leather jacket-clad Nvidia boss sitting next to a long-haired woman in glitzy jewellery believed to be Alice Huang. The following year, they both attended a dinner hosted by Jensen Huang at a Chinese restaurant in Taipei during Computex, the island's top tech expo. Journalists stood outside the restaurant filming through glass windows and doors as Jensen Huang and a woman identified as Alice Huang, who was wearing a pink dress, mingled with other attendees. At one point, Jensen Huang can be seen putting his arm around Alice Huang as she kisses him on the right cheek, press livestreams show. Alice Huang is also seen following the Nvidia chief as he re-enters the restaurant after talking to journalists outside, running her fingers down his lower back. They later leave the restaurant in the same car. US officials concluded last year that Alice Huang was targeting Jensen Huang as a spy, according to the New York Times and the Wall Street Journal. At the time, Alice Huang was said to be a top executive at data centre firm Megaspeed International, which rents out computing power to other companies to train and run AI. Megaspeed's website says it is "a core business partner of Nvidia's computing power cloud business in the Asia-Pacific region". On LinkedIn, it says it has offices in Singapore, Malaysia and Indonesia, with around two to 10 employees and 25 "associated members". When AFP called the number listed on Megaspeed's website, the person who answered said they were unfamiliar with the company and that the number was a residential line. The firm was previously called 7Road International, according to the Singapore government's website, suggesting links to Chinese gaming company 7Road. Washington restricts the export to China of Nvidia's most cutting-edge silicon chips, citing national security concerns but also seen as a measure to stay ahead in AI. The New York Times said the US government had been probing Megaspeed since 2024 over its potential steering of Nvidia chips to China. The company has also reportedly been under investigation by Singapore authorities, who the Times says questioned Alice Huang in 2025. AFP has contacted Singapore's police and the home affairs ministry for comment. Last year Bloomberg News also reported on the Singaporean probe into Megaspeed over the alleged smuggling of Nvidia chips to China. In December 2025, Megaspeed said Bloomberg's reporting "contains misleading information and incorrect insinuations, including suggestions that we may have been involved in illegal chip transfers". One of the Artificial Intelligence (AI) industry's most important figures has been accused of having an affair with a suspected Chinese spy. US intelligence officials believed that Chinese businesswoman Alice Huang, who had a close relationship with Nvidia chief executive and co-founder Jensen Huang, was a spy for Beijing , according to a New York Times report. Jensen Huang admitted , external to having been "unfaithful" to his wife and apologised for hurting her and their children. Nvidia, one of the most valuable companies in the world, has opened an independent investigation into the affair. It said it does not believe US national security had been compromised - and added that Jensen Huang is committed to continuing to lead the company. Here is what we know about the affair and why it matters. Jensen Huang (left) and Alice Huang - also known as Huang Le - at an event Alice Huang, no relation to Jensen Huang, was a top executive at Singapore-based data centre firm Megaspeed between March and November 2023. The company had been suspected of helping divert Nvidia chips to China. Nvidia said this was investigated and debunked. However, Megaspeed is under investigation by the Singapore government regarding previous allegations that the company was circumventing US sanctions on the export of Nvidia's high-end chips. Foreign Ministry spokesperson Guo Jiakun said: "The allegations about Chinese spies are entirely groundless, speculative and intended to smear and malign China." There were media reports in October that US President Donald Trump had been briefed last year on intelligence alleging Alice Huang was spying on China's behalf. US Secretary of State Marco Rubio, meanwhile, refused to comment when asked about Jensen Huang. In spring this year, the secretary of state reportedly oversaw the drafting of a memo that warned the Trump administration about Jensen Huang's relationship with the Chinese businesswoman. Trump says FBI investigating Nvidia boss's affair with alleged Chinese spy Zoe Kleinman: Nvidia CEO's affair will cause ripples across US and beyond Nvidia hires major New York law firm to investigate Jensen Huang affair Nvidia is at the heart of US and China's AI race , which is why the billionaire boss's affair has sparked national security fears among American lawmakers. Trump has said "whoever wins AI wins", and the concern is that if China gains the upper hand in AI, it will supercharge the country's military and surveillance capabilities. The US advantage is in large part because of companies like Nvidia, working with producers such as the Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company (TSMC), which makes more than 90% of the world's most advanced chips. Since 2022, the US has used various export controls to keep the top tech out of China, which it says helps retain America's competitive edge and protects its national security. This means companies like Nvidia have been largely locked out of the world's most lucrative market, with Jensen Huang once saying that Nvidia's share of the Chinese market had gone from around 95% to effectively zero. Jensen Huang has engaged in shuttle diplomacy between Washington and Beijing, hoping to find a US-approved way back in, and shaping US policy on China along the way. The revelations may explain why Jensen Huang has failed to bring home the biggest prize of all to Nvidia: the Trump administration's blessing to sell all but its most advanced chips to China . Born in Taiwan in 1963, Jensen Huang was nine years old when his family moved to the West Coast of the US. He graduated as an electrical engineer from Oregon State University, and then with a master's degree in the same field from Stanford University. He worked at US chip firm AMD before co-founding Nvidia. Known as "Daddy Huang" in Taiwan and once lauded as the "Taylor Swift of tech" , he has a reputation as a workaholic with incredibly high standards for his staff. He has an estimated fortune of $155bn (£115bn), according to the Bloomberg Billionaires Index. "Jensen Huang is a tech visionary of the likes of Steve Jobs," Stephen Witt, the author of Thinking Machine, a biography on the Jensen Huang, told the BBC, adding that he was responsible for creating AI hardware as we know it today. The Nvidia co-founder has a famously close relationship with Trump. At the recent AI summit at the White House, where 42 tech executives were present, the president was flanked by Elon Musk and Jensen Huang. Trump said he spoke with Jensen Huang after reports emerged about Alice Huang and her alledged links to the Chinese state and asked him: "'Did you have any idea she was a spy? "He said 'I had no idea she was a spy' and I really believe him," said Trump. Nvidia has launched an independent investigation into the affair and has hired New York law firm Wachtell, Lipton, Rosen & Katz. It will be led by Joon Kim, a former US Attorney for New York's Southern District who is now at litigation partner at the law firm. Jensen Huang has also been asked to appear for a joint closed-door briefing for several Congressional committees on 18 November. Members of the US House Foreign Affairs Committee asked the Nvidia chief executive to appear to explain his interactions with Alice Huang, as well as Nvidia's security protocols around espionage.

extraction.body: Tech executive Alice Huang is the woman accused of spying for China during an affair with Jensen Huang, head of US artificial intelligence chip titan Nvidia, according to media reports. Public details are sparse about the woman, also known as Huang Le, who had reportedly been a top figure at a Singapore-based data centre company called Megaspeed International. Here is what we know about her and the company: Alice Huang is a Chinese citizen recruited by Beijing to collect intelligence on the Nvidia boss, according to the New York Times, which first reported that Jensen Huang was the alleged target of a spy plot. Despite their shared surname, Alice Huang is no relation to the 63-year-old Taiwanese-born head of the world's most valuable company. The Times, citing people briefed on the surveillance, said that Alice Huang speaks good English and is well connected at the highest level of the global AI chip industry. The sector is highly sensitive as the United States and China race to develop advanced AI systems with potential military applications. An online search brought up a short profile for Alice Huang, with her photo, on a Chinese fund database. It listed previous jobs including at HSBC bank, and as a reporter for Chinese media outlets CCTV and Hunan TV. AFP was unable to verify the contents of the profile, or who had written it, but has attempted to contact the companies cited. Media reports last week said they had a close relationship, and Jensen Huang told Nvidia employees on Sunday he was "deeply sorry" for being "unfaithful to my wife". One photo from an industry party in 2024, posted on LinkedIn, appears to show the leather jacket-clad Nvidia boss sitting next to a long-haired woman in glitzy jewellery believed to be Alice Huang. The following year, they both attended a dinner hosted by Jensen Huang at a Chinese restaurant in Taipei during Computex, the island's top tech expo. Journalists stood outside the restaurant filming through glass windows and doors as Jensen Huang and a woman identified as Alice Huang, who was wearing a pink dress, mingled with other attendees. At one point, Jensen Huang can be seen putting his arm around Alice Huang as she kisses him on the right cheek, press livestreams show. Alice Huang is also seen following the Nvidia chief as he re-enters the restaurant after talking to journalists outside, running her fingers down his lower back. They later leave the restaurant in the same car. US officials concluded last year that Alice Huang was targeting Jensen Huang as a spy, according to the New York Times and the Wall Street Journal. At the time, Alice Huang was said to be a top executive at data centre firm Megaspeed International, which rents out computing power to other companies to train and run AI. Megaspeed's website says it is "a core business partner of Nvidia's computing power cloud business in the Asia-Pacific region". On LinkedIn, it says it has offices in Singapore, Malaysia and Indonesia, with around two to 10 employees and 25 "associated members". When AFP called the number listed on Megaspeed's website, the person who answered said they were unfamiliar with the company and that the number was a residential line. The firm was previously called 7Road International, according to the Singapore government's website, suggesting links to Chinese gaming company 7Road. Washington restricts the export to China of Nvidia's most cutting-edge silicon chips, citing national security concerns but also seen as a measure to stay ahead in AI. The New York Times said the US government had been probing Megaspeed since 2024 over its potential steering of Nvidia chips to China. The company has also reportedly been under investigation by Singapore authorities, who the Times says questioned Alice Huang in 2025. AFP has contacted Singapore's police and the home affairs ministry for comment. Last year Bloomberg News also reported on the Singaporean probe into Megaspeed over the alleged smuggling of Nvidia chips to China. In December 2025, Megaspeed said Bloomberg's reporting "contains misleading information and incorrect insinuations, including suggestions that we may have been involved in illegal chip transfers". extraction.body: Google has introduced Tabletop, a new Google Labs experiment designed to help groups create customized interactive planning tools and collaborate in real time. The platform allows users to combine links, files, and ideas with AI-powered prompts to generate shared experiences, including travel itineraries, dinner polls, expense splitters, and tournament brackets. Announced on November 11, 2026, Tabletop is designed to simplify activities that require coordination among multiple participants. The experiment brings group planning and interactive tool creation into a shared digital workspace, allowing participants to organize information, make decisions, and collaborate without relying on multiple separate applications. Tabletop is initially rolling out in the United States through a waitlist for users aged 18 and older. The announcement was made by Roman Nurik, Design and Engineering Lead at Google Labs. Tabletop allows users to create customized collaborative spaces based on their specific activities and requirements. Rather than requiring participants to use predetermined planning formats, the platform can generate interactive tools from information provided by users. To begin, users add relevant links, upload files, or describe their ideas within a Tabletop workspace. They can then enter instructions using the @tabletop prompt interface to generate an interactive planning experience. Alternatively, users can select a starter template designed around a common group activity. For example, a group organizing a vacation can create an interactive travel itinerary that brings together planning information in one location. Participants coordinating a dinner can generate a poll to collect preferences and make decisions collaboratively. Groups managing shared expenses can create tools to divide costs among participants. Tabletop can also generate tournament brackets for recreational leagues, competitions, and other organized activities. These examples illustrate how the platform is intended to support different types of collaborative planning without requiring users to develop software themselves. Real-Time Collaboration Through Shared Workspaces A central feature of Tabletop is its support for simultaneous participation. Once a workspace has been created, users can share an invitation link through an existing group chat. Other participants can then enter the workspace and interact with its tools at the same time. Google compares this collaborative experience to Google Docs, where multiple people can contribute to a shared document simultaneously. Tabletop extends the concept beyond text editing by allowing groups to interact with customized planning tools. This approach is designed to reduce the coordination challenges associated with organizing group activities across separate messages, spreadsheets, documents, and websites. For instance, organizing a family vacation can require collecting destination information, coordinating schedules, discussing activities, and making group decisions. Tabletop is intended to bring these activities into a common environment where participants can contribute directly. The same model can support recreational sports leagues, social gatherings, and other activities involving shared decisions. Tabletop is being introduced through Google Labs, the company’s platform for testing experimental technologies and product concepts. The project reflects Google’s exploration of AI-powered interfaces that allow users to create customized digital experiences through natural-language instructions. Rather than offering only a conventional chatbot interaction, Tabletop uses AI to help generate interactive tools that groups can use collaboratively. Its focus is on transforming user-provided information into practical planning experiences. The ability to incorporate links, files, and ideas allows the platform to adapt to different activities and group requirements. Google has not announced a general availability date beyond the initial U.S. waitlist rollout. The company has also not provided detailed information about future pricing, supported integrations, or international availability. For now, the experiment is available to eligible U.S. adults through a waitlist. Tabletop represents Google’s effort to make AI-generated interactive experiences useful for everyday group coordination, combining natural-language customization with the real-time collaboration familiar from existing productivity applications. By allowing users to create shared planning tools without building them manually, Google is exploring a new approach to organizing activities, coordinating decisions, and helping groups work together.

sources.title: Google: Tabletop Launches As AI-Powered Collaborative Planning Tool For Groups - Pulse 2.0
passages: Google has introduced Tabletop, a new Google Labs experiment designed to help groups create customized interactive planning tools and collaborate in real time.

The platform allows users to combine links, files, and ideas with AI-powered prompts to generate shared experiences, including travel itineraries, dinner polls, expense splitters, and tournament brackets.

Tabletop represents Google’s effort to make AI-generated interactive experiences useful for everyday group coordination, combining natural-language customization with the real-time collaboration familiar from existing productivity applications.
Google compares this collaborative experience to Google Docs, where multiple people can contribute to a shared document simultaneously.

The experiment brings group planning and interactive tool creation into a shared digital workspace, allowing participants to organize information, make decisions, and collaborate without relying on multiple separate applications.
Tabletop extends the concept beyond text editing by allowing groups to interact with customized planning tools.
Tabletop is being introduced through Google Labs, the company’s platform for testing experimental technologies and product concepts.
Google has not announced a general availability date beyond the initial U.S. waitlist rollout.
Groups managing shared expenses can create tools to divide costs among participants.
They can then enter instructions using the @tabletop prompt interface to generate an interactive planning experience.
For example, a group organizing a vacation can create an interactive travel itinerary that brings together planning information in one location.
Rather than offering only a conventional chatbot interaction, Tabletop uses AI to help generate interactive tools that groups can use collaboratively.

extraction.body: Google has introduced Tabletop, a new Google Labs experiment designed to help groups create customized interactive planning tools and collaborate in real time. The platform allows users to combine links, files, and ideas with AI-powered prompts to generate shared experiences, including travel itineraries, dinner polls, expense splitters, and tournament brackets. Announced on November 11, 2026, Tabletop is designed to simplify activities that require coordination among multiple participants. The experiment brings group planning and interactive tool creation into a shared digital workspace, allowing participants to organize information, make decisions, and collaborate without relying on multiple separate applications. Tabletop is initially rolling out in the United States through a waitlist for users aged 18 and older. The announcement was made by Roman Nurik, Design and Engineering Lead at Google Labs. Tabletop allows users to create customized collaborative spaces based on their specific activities and requirements. Rather than requiring participants to use predetermined planning formats, the platform can generate interactive tools from information provided by users. To begin, users add relevant links, upload files, or describe their ideas within a Tabletop workspace. They can then enter instructions using the @tabletop prompt interface to generate an interactive planning experience. Alternatively, users can select a starter template designed around a common group activity. For example, a group organizing a vacation can create an interactive travel itinerary that brings together planning information in one location. Participants coordinating a dinner can generate a poll to collect preferences and make decisions collaboratively. Groups managing shared expenses can create tools to divide costs among participants. Tabletop can also generate tournament brackets for recreational leagues, competitions, and other organized activities. These examples illustrate how the platform is intended to support different types of collaborative planning without requiring users to develop software themselves. Real-Time Collaboration Through Shared Workspaces A central feature of Tabletop is its support for simultaneous participation. Once a workspace has been created, users can share an invitation link through an existing group chat. Other participants can then enter the workspace and interact with its tools at the same time. Google compares this collaborative experience to Google Docs, where multiple people can contribute to a shared document simultaneously. Tabletop extends the concept beyond text editing by allowing groups to interact with customized planning tools. This approach is designed to reduce the coordination challenges associated with organizing group activities across separate messages, spreadsheets, documents, and websites. For instance, organizing a family vacation can require collecting destination information, coordinating schedules, discussing activities, and making group decisions. Tabletop is intended to bring these activities into a common environment where participants can contribute directly. The same model can support recreational sports leagues, social gatherings, and other activities involving shared decisions. Tabletop is being introduced through Google Labs, the company’s platform for testing experimental technologies and product concepts. The project reflects Google’s exploration of AI-powered interfaces that allow users to create customized digital experiences through natural-language instructions. Rather than offering only a conventional chatbot interaction, Tabletop uses AI to help generate interactive tools that groups can use collaboratively. Its focus is on transforming user-provided information into practical planning experiences. The ability to incorporate links, files, and ideas allows the platform to adapt to different activities and group requirements. Google has not announced a general availability date beyond the initial U.S. waitlist rollout. The company has also not provided detailed information about future pricing, supported integrations, or international availability. For now, the experiment is available to eligible U.S. adults through a waitlist. Tabletop represents Google’s effort to make AI-generated interactive experiences useful for everyday group coordination, combining natural-language customization with the real-time collaboration familiar from existing productivity applications. By allowing users to create shared planning tools without building them manually, Google is exploring a new approach to organizing activities, coordinating decisions, and helping groups work together.

sources.title: Congress could issue subpoena to Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang if he doesn’t respond by today to request for a ‘joint, closed-door briefing’ — US representatives want to discuss company’s ‘security protocols against foreign adversary espionage’ - Tom's Hardware
passages: Brian Mast (R-Fla.), the chairperson of the House Foreign Affairs Committee, has said that he will issue a subpoena to Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang if he does not respond to the committee’s request to meet with them on November 18 by Wednesday, November 11, according to ABC News .

Congress first called the embattled CEO on November 7, a few days after rumors started circulating about Huang’s “closeness” to a particular Chinese executive suspected of passing information to Chinese intelligence.

The following day, Nvidia released a statement from Jensen admitting to an affair with Megaspeed executive Alice Huang, apologizing for his unfaithfulness, while the company’s board of directors confirmed it will launch an independent investigation regarding the allegations that the CEO has been specifically targeted by China’s Ministry of State Security (MSS).
Aside from having to face Congress, Jensen Huang is also reportedly being looked into by the FBI.
Tom's Hardware is part of Future US Inc, an international media group and leading digital publisher.
It remains unclear whether Jensen Huang was targeted by intelligence agencies, but he came into prominence with the AI boom that was arguably fueled by Nvidia’s AI chips.
We also don’t know if Huang Le or Alice Huang is actually a Chinese spy or an “innocent” bystander caught in a web of accusations.
A former CIA agent says that Jensen Huang had a target on his back, and that other engineers and executives could have also be approached by Chinese spies.

The House invited him to a “joint, closed-door briefing” with the heads of the House committees on China, Foreign Affairs, and Intelligence, and that they will focus on his company’s “ security protocols against foreign adversary espionage.” Congress first called the embattled CEO on November 7, a few days after rumors started circulating about Huang’s “closeness” to a particular Chinese executive suspected of passing information to Chinese intelligence. We also don’t know if Huang Le or Alice Huang is actually a Chinese spy or an “innocent” bystander caught in a web of accusations. Are they talking to the engineers? Are they talking to other people who might have even more access than even the CEO has? So, this focus should not be singular; it should include everyone in the company, and quite frankly, every tech company out there should be looking at all the contacts that their officers and employees have.” “It’s definitely not a one-time thing. When you run a trillion-dollar company, you know that you have a bullseye on your back; whether it’s from competition or rather from nation-states, so this is absolutely not a one-off. Brian Mast (R-Fla.), the chairperson of the House Foreign Affairs Committee, has said that he will issue a subpoena to Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang if he does not respond to the committee’s request to meet with them on November 18 by Wednesday, November 11, according to ABC News . The House invited him to a “joint, closed-door briefing” with the heads of the House committees on China, Foreign Affairs, and Intelligence, and that they will focus on his company’s “ security protocols against foreign adversary espionage.”

Congress first called the embattled CEO on November 7, a few days after rumors started circulating about Huang’s “closeness” to a particular Chinese executive suspected of passing information to Chinese intelligence. The following day, Nvidia released a statement from Jensen admitting to an affair with Megaspeed executive Alice Huang, apologizing for his unfaithfulness, while the company’s board of directors confirmed it will launch an independent investigation regarding the allegations that the CEO has been specifically targeted by China’s Ministry of State Security (MSS). Aside from having to face Congress, Jensen Huang is also reportedly being looked into by the FBI.

It remains unclear whether Jensen Huang was targeted by intelligence agencies, but he came into prominence with the AI boom that was arguably fueled by Nvidia’s AI chips. This led to the AI race as we know it today, with the U.S. taking steps to delay China’s advancement for fears that it will use the technology for military purposes. We also don’t know if Huang Le or Alice Huang is actually a Chinese spy or an “innocent” bystander caught in a web of accusations. And, even if she did work with the MSS, the question remains as to whether she specifically targeted the Nvidia CEO or whether Chinese intelligence discovered their indiscretion and used that as a convenient tool for blackmail to extract information from her.

However, former CIA agent Darrel Blocker told ABC News that the authorities should just focus on Jensen. “I think that the biggest concern is that the focus or overfocus on just Jensen Huang and Nvidia risks losing sight of the fact that other people have been targeted by the Chinese. Are they talking to the engineers? Are they talking to other people who might have even more access than even the CEO has? So, this focus should not be singular; it should include everyone in the company, and quite frankly, every tech company out there should be looking at all the contacts that their officers and employees have.”

“It’s definitely not a one-time thing. When you run a trillion-dollar company, you know that you have a bullseye on your back; whether it’s from competition or rather from nation-states, so this is absolutely not a one-off. Jensen Huang is not the only person at Nvidia that has access to the crown jewels, so I would be looking at the other people in terms of the access that they enjoy and their proximity to Chinese nationals.”

extraction.body: They’re the first two products from the company’s new autonomous home security devices category. It's been at least six years since Amazon first teased an in-home security camera in the form of a drone, but Ring founder Jamie Siminoff says that his company has actually been working on a "drone concept" since 2016. That's before Amazon even acquired Ring in 2018 , and about a decade in the making. After some starts and stops, including the various reveals and tests over the years, Siminoff believes the Ring Drone Cam is finally ready for the general public. It will retail for $249.99 and ship on January 27, 2027. The camera is part of a pair of devices launching as part of the Ring Robotics "category of autonomous, mobile security" that Amazon is also unveiling today. The Ring Drone Cam weighs 165 grams (0.36 pounds) and is basically a tiny quadcopter with cameras onboard. It has a 2K camera and two LEDs on its front and a 1080p camera on the underside. There's also an LED at the bottom for illumination. These lights don't just help illuminate in low light or in dark corners, but can also provide a deterrent to would-be intruders at night. Ring's executives said that when the Drone Cam is flying around your darkened home, its moving lights can resemble the action of a security guard holding up a flashlight and looking around. The Drone Cam can fly on your preconfigured schedules, as if it's on patrol, or it can chart a flight path in response to a motion sensor or leak sensor that's gone off somewhere in your home. You can also manually start a flight whenever you want, of course. All this is made a bit easier thanks to the Alexa Home Map that Amazon first announced last month, which provides a 3D map view of your house. Instead of having to control and navigate the device, you can just tap a spot on the map and the Drone Cam will chart its own course to the destination. Amazon said the device's battery will support about eight to 10 minutes of air time, depending on the altitude of the path (as it impacts how hard the propellers have to spin). When it's about to run out of juice or can't connect to Wi-Fi, the Ring Drone Cam will simply land or return to its dock, where eight minutes of charging will deliver enough power for 1 minute of flight time. Siminoff said at a media briefing in New York this week that previous iterations of the Drone Cam simply weren't good enough to launch to the public. After the first drone was announced in 2021, the company put products in boxes but never shipped them out, because, according to Siminoff, they "just didn't work well enough." Another false start happened in 2025, and the company was finding problems that required more sensors and "more compute," which then demanded more power and bigger batteries. With the added weight, the drone had to "fly harder," which created safety concerns that led to larger shrouds. That then impacted flight performance as less air could get through. Finally, to do all that in a device would probably drive its retail price up past $5,000, Siminoff said. That would mean it wouldn't really be right for consumers. What allowed Ring to drop the Drone Cam's weight and price was cloud-processing and what Siminoff calls "intelligence." And it sounds like the company is calling it the "AI Pilot," which powers both the Ring Drone Cam and the Rover Cam (which I'll get to in a bit). That system basically "maps the space, suggests patrol points, and autonomously navigates around obstacles," according to a Ring press release. This is basically cloud processing to tell the drone where to go when a motion detector goes off, for instance. So instead of requiring a local AI model and the processors to run those, the Drone Cam is mostly reliant on Wi-Fi. Of course, as with other Ring cameras, privacy is a major concern for anyone considering this drone. Amazon said "Privacy isn't just a feature of Ring Robotics; it is the default." When the drone is in its base, it will power down and turn off its camera, only recording when "a flight is triggered." The company said that videos from both the Drone Cam and the Rover Cam "will be protected by TAKE (Throw Away the Key Encryption), Ring's strongest default encryption yet." Amazon also launched the Ring Rover Cam today, and those who are familiar with the parent company's previous robotic products may find it familiar. It's basically the Astro robot that was announced in 2021 and slowly morphed into a security robot . The business version of that, which cost $2,350, was discontinued in 2024 but has now been resurrected as a $1,000... security robot. The similarity between Astro and the new Rover Cam is not a coincidence. Ring even said the Rover Cam "was originally inspired by feedback from Amazon Astro customers who said the feature they loved most was roving security." On the outside the Rover Cam looks nearly identical to the Astro. It has a tablet for a face and a vertical camera above the screen that looks like a chunky antenna. Its body comprises a round wheel-shaped housing glued onto a small rectangular butt with a light tower at the top of its back. The Rover Cam is designed for use in enterprise scenarios like warehouse monitoring or patrolling of spaces as needed by small to medium businesses. Like the Drone Cam, it can go to a specific destination, automatically respond to disturbances or patrol customized routes on a schedule. To improve its view, the Rover can spin 360 degrees, and its camera can extend up to 4 feet on a periscope. The Rover has a few additional features, like a higher-resolution 4K camera, a built-in siren that was something I heard very easily at a demo from more than 10 feet away. Its light tower not only projects a blue ring onto the ceiling so you can quickly locate it, but also flashes red when the siren is going off. It also has a built-in speaker and microphone so you can speak and listen to people through the device. It can also stream and record while it's en route to check on something, not just when it's arrived at its destination. Finally, even when the Rover is docked, it is continuously watching for "person motion," according to the company's press release and start recording "the moment it detects motion in its view." Both the Rover and Drone cameras work with the Alexa Home Map that Amazon first announced last month . The software releases along with the Rover Cam on December 16, and it'll feature a more photorealistic rendering than we saw at launch. With this interface, users can just tap a spot on their home or office to send the robot out. As another part of Ring Robotics' privacy features, both devices "are designed to be seen and heard." The Ring Drone is, well, an obviously flying object but it also is loud. Its propellers were pretty noisy, based on what I saw at a recent demo, and you'll most likely not want to have it flying for more than a few minutes in your home if you want to live in peace. As for the Rover Cam, Amazon said its "light tower is bright and easy to spot" and that "if someone's there who shouldn't be, a flying drone overhead or a roving robot with a siren makes it clear they've been spotted." In this way, the company said, the "devices are built to deter, not just monitor."

passages: Amazon’s Ring launched Ring Robotics on 10 November: the $249.99 Ring Drone Cam, a flying indoor camera, and the $999.99 Ring Rover Cam.
Amazon will begin shipping the Drone Cam in the US on 27 January 2027, but only if the FCC authorises it.
Amazon launched Astro for Business in November 2023 from $2,350, then discontinued it less than a year later, refunding customers and shutting the robots off.
The original Astro for the home remains invite-only, and CNBC reported that Amazon has moved much of the Astro team to a new home robot.
Scheduled flights and patrols, and reviewing the Rover’s recorded video, require a Ring Protect plan.
Ring hasn’t said which plans qualify or what they’ll cost.
Siminoff told TechRadar: “It’s loud — we think that’s a feature.” The noise is meant to warn people, so the drone isn’t meant to sneak up on anyone.
When a Ring camera, sensor, or alarm trips, it flies to previously set patrol points to investigate, so one drone can cover spots that would otherwise need several fixed cameras.
Owners can also schedule routes or send it out on demand.
It records 2K video with a 148° field of view, rotates 360°, and has two LED lights for low light.
It patrols autonomously, streams and records in up to 4K, and has a periscope camera, a siren, a light tower, and two-way audio.
The Verge puts its battery life at about 30 minutes, covering around 5,000 square feet on one floor.
Ring’s founder and chief inventor, Jamie Siminoff, frames the launch as a break from more cameras.

extraction.body: Amazon has announced the Ring Drone Cam, a flying indoor security camera that patrols your home. You might be thinking this is old news, and you wouldn't be mistaken. You see, the company showed off an indoor security drone called the Always Home Cam back in September 2020 and promised it would ship the following year. It rolled out to a small group of U.S. buyers on an invite-only basis in late 2021 but never made it to general release, and disappeared in 2024. So the new Ring Drone Cam arrives with something to prove. This time there's a price and a shipping date attached to the camera. It costs $249.99 and will start shipping in the U.S. from January 27, 2027. It launches next to the Ring Rover Cam, a $999.99 wheeled patrol robot built for businesses that borrows its roving security trick from Amazon's Astro. Both products sit under a new arm of Ring that the company is calling Ring Robotics — suggesting there may be more on the way. Amazon says that the drone camera means you no longer need multiple cameras in your home, and can instead purchase this one device. If you've been weighing up one of the household robots already on sale , this is a good option for security rather than chores. When not in use, the Ring Drone Cam sits in a dock with its camera shuttered, lifts off when you tell it to (or when something sets it off), and flies the routes you've set. If one of your other Ring cameras, sensors, or alarms is triggered, the drone takes off by itself and heads to the area , so you can actually look at the room rather than just receive a notification about it. You can launch the Drone Cam on demand too, and it can be controlled with Alexa Home Map, the house-mapping feature Amazon introduced with the Echo Show 16 last month . To set up the Drone Cam, you will have to carry it around your home while it builds a floor plan, which is likely safer than trying to fly it around indoors. It'll then suggest spots in your home worth watching, such as a side door or the end of a corridor. Mapping and the in-flight navigation both run on a system that Ring calls AI Pilot, which uses the camera, onboard sensors, and cloud processing to steer around furniture it finds in the way. It records video in 2K across a 148-degree field of view, and the drone can rotate a full 360 degrees to cover an entire room from one position. It has two built-in LEDs, which can switch on by themselves in low light. For many, a camera that follows you around your own house is a harder sell than one bolted to a wall. Given the privacy trade-offs that come with any Ring camera , and the fact that Amazon — a company that doesn't exactly have the best reputation when it comes to privacy — has already had to answer for how staff handled customer camera feeds , it perhaps matters more on this camera than others. But the company has clearly put some thought into making the Drone Cam as privacy-friendly as it can be, with a number of features to provide peace of mind. The camera stays off while docked, and there is a physical shutter. The drone only records once it's airborne, and an LED tells you when it's rolling. The propellers are audible by design — so much so, The Verge described the Drone Cam as "noisy as heck" — which Ring frames as a deterrent. Although I can't help but think that it doubles as a warning for any intruders in your home who would also rather not be filmed. Footage is covered by Throw Away the Key encryption, which Ring describes as its strongest default encryption yet. The scheduled flight routes and video review features both require a paid Ring Protect subscription plan to operate, so $249.99 isn't the whole cost of the Drone Cam. The product announcement also mentions the new device hasn't yet been authorized under Federal Communications Commission rules and can't be sold or leased until it is. So although it's providing a January shipping date, I'd treat this as a target rather than a guarantee. The Rover Cam, which carries no such caveat, will ship earlier on December 16, 2026.

coreStoryFacts.text: Ring first showed off its Drone Cam in 2020 , but never actually brought the product to market.
That changes in January of next year, when the Ring Drone Cam will be available for $249.99.

The camera, Amazon expains, is “a flying indoor security camera that goes where you need it, when you need it, and stays docked and out of sight when you don’t.” You can set flight routes on a schedule, have the drone automatically investigate tripped sensors in your Ring system, and more.
The other robot Amazon’s Ring is launching is the Rover Cam, which is built on the back of Amazon Astro.
It also features two-way audio and a built-in siren to deter intruders from an area, while also features continuous 4K recording.
Indoor cameras can be invaluable for securing your home, but also just in keeping an eye on what’s going on when you’re not home.
Ring is mainly pitching this one for businesses, and it costs $999.99 with pre-orders open now ahead of a December 16 release date.

It's been at least six years since Amazon first teased an in-home security camera in the form of a drone, but Ring founder Jamie Siminoff says that his company has actually been working on a "drone concept" since 2016.
That's before Amazon even acquired Ring in 2018 , and about a decade in the making.
After some starts and stops, including the various reveals and tests over the years, Siminoff believes the Ring Drone Cam is finally ready for the general public.
The camera is part of a pair of devices launching as part of the Ring Robotics "category of autonomous, mobile security" that Amazon is also unveiling today.
Of course, as with other Ring cameras, privacy is a major concern for anyone considering this drone.

Amazon said "Privacy isn't just a feature of Ring Robotics; it is the default." When the drone is in its base, it will power down and turn off its camera, only recording when "a flight is triggered." The company said that videos from both the Drone Cam and the Rover Cam "will be protected by TAKE (Throw Away the Key Encryption), Ring's strongest default encryption yet."
Amazon also launched the Ring Rover Cam today, and those who are familiar with the parent company's previous robotic products may find it familiar.

extraction.body: They’re the first two products from the company’s new autonomous home security devices category. It's been at least six years since Amazon first teased an in-home security camera in the form of a drone, but Ring founder Jamie Siminoff says that his company has actually been working on a "drone concept" since 2016. That's before Amazon even acquired Ring in 2018 , and about a decade in the making. After some starts and stops, including the various reveals and tests over the years, Siminoff believes the Ring Drone Cam is finally ready for the general public. It will retail for $249.99 and ship on January 27, 2027. The camera is part of a pair of devices launching as part of the Ring Robotics "category of autonomous, mobile security" that Amazon is also unveiling today. The Ring Drone Cam weighs 165 grams (0.36 pounds) and is basically a tiny quadcopter with cameras onboard. It has a 2K camera and two LEDs on its front and a 1080p camera on the underside. There's also an LED at the bottom for illumination. These lights don't just help illuminate in low light or in dark corners, but can also provide a deterrent to would-be intruders at night. Ring's executives said that when the Drone Cam is flying around your darkened home, its moving lights can resemble the action of a security guard holding up a flashlight and looking around. The Drone Cam can fly on your preconfigured schedules, as if it's on patrol, or it can chart a flight path in response to a motion sensor or leak sensor that's gone off somewhere in your home. You can also manually start a flight whenever you want, of course. All this is made a bit easier thanks to the Alexa Home Map that Amazon first announced last month, which provides a 3D map view of your house. Instead of having to control and navigate the device, you can just tap a spot on the map and the Drone Cam will chart its own course to the destination. Amazon said the device's battery will support about eight to 10 minutes of air time, depending on the altitude of the path (as it impacts how hard the propellers have to spin). When it's about to run out of juice or can't connect to Wi-Fi, the Ring Drone Cam will simply land or return to its dock, where eight minutes of charging will deliver enough power for 1 minute of flight time. Siminoff said at a media briefing in New York this week that previous iterations of the Drone Cam simply weren't good enough to launch to the public. After the first drone was announced in 2021, the company put products in boxes but never shipped them out, because, according to Siminoff, they "just didn't work well enough." Another false start happened in 2025, and the company was finding problems that required more sensors and "more compute," which then demanded more power and bigger batteries. With the added weight, the drone had to "fly harder," which created safety concerns that led to larger shrouds. That then impacted flight performance as less air could get through. Finally, to do all that in a device would probably drive its retail price up past $5,000, Siminoff said. That would mean it wouldn't really be right for consumers. What allowed Ring to drop the Drone Cam's weight and price was cloud-processing and what Siminoff calls "intelligence." And it sounds like the company is calling it the "AI Pilot," which powers both the Ring Drone Cam and the Rover Cam (which I'll get to in a bit). That system basically "maps the space, suggests patrol points, and autonomously navigates around obstacles," according to a Ring press release. This is basically cloud processing to tell the drone where to go when a motion detector goes off, for instance. So instead of requiring a local AI model and the processors to run those, the Drone Cam is mostly reliant on Wi-Fi. Of course, as with other Ring cameras, privacy is a major concern for anyone considering this drone. Amazon said "Privacy isn't just a feature of Ring Robotics; it is the default." When the drone is in its base, it will power down and turn off its camera, only recording when "a flight is triggered." The company said that videos from both the Drone Cam and the Rover Cam "will be protected by TAKE (Throw Away the Key Encryption), Ring's strongest default encryption yet." Amazon also launched the Ring Rover Cam today, and those who are familiar with the parent company's previous robotic products may find it familiar. It's basically the Astro robot that was announced in 2021 and slowly morphed into a security robot . The business version of that, which cost $2,350, was discontinued in 2024 but has now been resurrected as a $1,000... security robot. The similarity between Astro and the new Rover Cam is not a coincidence. Ring even said the Rover Cam "was originally inspired by feedback from Amazon Astro customers who said the feature they loved most was roving security." On the outside the Rover Cam looks nearly identical to the Astro. It has a tablet for a face and a vertical camera above the screen that looks like a chunky antenna. Its body comprises a round wheel-shaped housing glued onto a small rectangular butt with a light tower at the top of its back. The Rover Cam is designed for use in enterprise scenarios like warehouse monitoring or patrolling of spaces as needed by small to medium businesses. Like the Drone Cam, it can go to a specific destination, automatically respond to disturbances or patrol customized routes on a schedule. To improve its view, the Rover can spin 360 degrees, and its camera can extend up to 4 feet on a periscope. The Rover has a few additional features, like a higher-resolution 4K camera, a built-in siren that was something I heard very easily at a demo from more than 10 feet away. Its light tower not only projects a blue ring onto the ceiling so you can quickly locate it, but also flashes red when the siren is going off. It also has a built-in speaker and microphone so you can speak and listen to people through the device. It can also stream and record while it's en route to check on something, not just when it's arrived at its destination. Finally, even when the Rover is docked, it is continuously watching for "person motion," according to the company's press release and start recording "the moment it detects motion in its view." Both the Rover and Drone cameras work with the Alexa Home Map that Amazon first announced last month . The software releases along with the Rover Cam on December 16, and it'll feature a more photorealistic rendering than we saw at launch. With this interface, users can just tap a spot on their home or office to send the robot out. As another part of Ring Robotics' privacy features, both devices "are designed to be seen and heard." The Ring Drone is, well, an obviously flying object but it also is loud. Its propellers were pretty noisy, based on what I saw at a recent demo, and you'll most likely not want to have it flying for more than a few minutes in your home if you want to live in peace. As for the Rover Cam, Amazon said its "light tower is bright and easy to spot" and that "if someone's there who shouldn't be, a flying drone overhead or a roving robot with a siren makes it clear they've been spotted." In this way, the company said, the "devices are built to deter, not just monitor."

passages: Amazon has announced the Ring Drone Cam, a flying indoor security camera that patrols your home.
You see, the company showed off an indoor security drone called the Always Home Cam back in September 2020 and promised it would ship the following year.
This time there's a price and a shipping date attached to the camera.
Amazon says that the drone camera means you no longer need multiple cameras in your home, and can instead purchase this one device.

If one of your other Ring cameras, sensors, or alarms is triggered, the drone takes off by itself and heads to the area , so you can actually look at the room rather than just receive a notification about it.

Given the privacy trade-offs that come with any Ring camera , and the fact that Amazon — a company that doesn't exactly have the best reputation when it comes to privacy — has already had to answer for how staff handled customer camera feeds , it perhaps matters more on this camera than others.
The propellers are audible by design — so much so, The Verge described the Drone Cam as "noisy as heck" — which Ring frames as a deterrent.
Mapping and the in-flight navigation both run on a system that Ring calls AI Pilot, which uses the camera, onboard sensors, and cloud processing to steer around furniture it finds in the way.

extraction.body: Amazon has announced the Ring Drone Cam, a flying indoor security camera that patrols your home. You might be thinking this is old news, and you wouldn't be mistaken. You see, the company showed off an indoor security drone called the Always Home Cam back in September 2020 and promised it would ship the following year. It rolled out to a small group of U.S. buyers on an invite-only basis in late 2021 but never made it to general release, and disappeared in 2024. So the new Ring Drone Cam arrives with something to prove. This time there's a price and a shipping date attached to the camera. It costs $249.99 and will start shipping in the U.S. from January 27, 2027. It launches next to the Ring Rover Cam, a $999.99 wheeled patrol robot built for businesses that borrows its roving security trick from Amazon's Astro. Both products sit under a new arm of Ring that the company is calling Ring Robotics — suggesting there may be more on the way. Amazon says that the drone camera means you no longer need multiple cameras in your home, and can instead purchase this one device. If you've been weighing up one of the household robots already on sale , this is a good option for security rather than chores. When not in use, the Ring Drone Cam sits in a dock with its camera shuttered, lifts off when you tell it to (or when something sets it off), and flies the routes you've set. If one of your other Ring cameras, sensors, or alarms is triggered, the drone takes off by itself and heads to the area , so you can actually look at the room rather than just receive a notification about it. You can launch the Drone Cam on demand too, and it can be controlled with Alexa Home Map, the house-mapping feature Amazon introduced with the Echo Show 16 last month . To set up the Drone Cam, you will have to carry it around your home while it builds a floor plan, which is likely safer than trying to fly it around indoors. It'll then suggest spots in your home worth watching, such as a side door or the end of a corridor. Mapping and the in-flight navigation both run on a system that Ring calls AI Pilot, which uses the camera, onboard sensors, and cloud processing to steer around furniture it finds in the way. It records video in 2K across a 148-degree field of view, and the drone can rotate a full 360 degrees to cover an entire room from one position. It has two built-in LEDs, which can switch on by themselves in low light. For many, a camera that follows you around your own house is a harder sell than one bolted to a wall. Given the privacy trade-offs that come with any Ring camera , and the fact that Amazon — a company that doesn't exactly have the best reputation when it comes to privacy — has already had to answer for how staff handled customer camera feeds , it perhaps matters more on this camera than others. But the company has clearly put some thought into making the Drone Cam as privacy-friendly as it can be, with a number of features to provide peace of mind. The camera stays off while docked, and there is a physical shutter. The drone only records once it's airborne, and an LED tells you when it's rolling. The propellers are audible by design — so much so, The Verge described the Drone Cam as "noisy as heck" — which Ring frames as a deterrent. Although I can't help but think that it doubles as a warning for any intruders in your home who would also rather not be filmed. Footage is covered by Throw Away the Key encryption, which Ring describes as its strongest default encryption yet. The scheduled flight routes and video review features both require a paid Ring Protect subscription plan to operate, so $249.99 isn't the whole cost of the Drone Cam. The product announcement also mentions the new device hasn't yet been authorized under Federal Communications Commission rules and can't be sold or leased until it is. So although it's providing a January shipping date, I'd treat this as a target rather than a guarantee. The Rover Cam, which carries no such caveat, will ship earlier on December 16, 2026.
