extraction.body: Nvidia co-founder CEO Jensen Huang has never been as flashy or controversy-prone as AI leaders like OpenAI’s Sam Altman or SpaceXAI’s Elon Musk. Now, the 63-year-old industry kingpin has admitted that he cheated on his wife of 40 years in an affair that could have ramifications beyond Huang’s personal life and potentially impact national security. United States officials believe that Huang’s likely romantic interest, Megaspeed executive Alice Huang, is a Chinese spy who has been feeding information back to Beijing. (Alice Huang, a Chinese citizen, is of no relation to Jensen Huang.) Megaspeed, a Singapore-based AI infrastructure company, had reportedly purchased $4.8 billion in Nvidia chips over the last two years. The U.S. and Singapore have both previously investigated Megaspeed over suspicions that the firm was illegally sharing chips with China. The Justice Department has since taken over the federal investigation into the company, the Times has reported. The story took a sudden new turn on Wednesday. Citing five people who worked at Nvidia, the Times reported that Huang also had an extramarital relationship with Kimberly Powell, the company’s vice president of health care, who reports directly to him. Nvidia, Huang and Powell have not confirmed the report. Reached by a Times reporter, Huang reportedly said, “I don’t think you should be talking to me directly,” before hanging up. Separately, the Wall Street Journal reported that Nvidia’s board is preparing to oust Huang , and Nvidia’s shares fell in after-hours trading. The U.S. and China are embroiled in a fierce technological arms race to build the most advanced AI infrastructure, which could shape each country’s economic future, military prowess, and capacity for innovation. Nvidia is valuable in this competition as one of the world’s largest makers of AI chips, which are essential for accelerating AI development. But as an American company, Nvidia faces government restrictions on the sale of its most powerful chips to Chinese entities. As the controversy unfolds, we are organizing the most relevant events into a reverse-chronological timeline to keep you up to date. After reports of a second extramarital affair, Nvidia’s board reportedly plans to meet to discuss Huang’s future at the company, per the Wall Street Journal. Stock fell about 8% in after hours trading on Wednesday and is down 11% in the past five days. Huang famously delegates very little and has about 60 direct reports, he has said . The company has not had an obvious successor or a succession plan. The New York Times reported that Jensen Huang also had an affair with Nvidia vice president of healthcare Kimberly Powell, who reports directly to the CEO. According to the report, Huang and Powell were captured on film “being affectionate” at a hotel during a conference earlier this year. Huang has not responded to a request from three Republican congressman to appear for a closed-door briefing for questioning about his affair with an alleged Chinese spy. House China committee Chairman Moolenaar said Wednesday on Fox Business that if Huang doesn’t agree to the briefing, he’ll likely be subpoenaed . The Nvidia CEO pulled out of upcoming speaking engagements at the ElevenLabs Summit and Anthropic CEO Forum. Alice Huang and her family reportedly built a network of companies in China and Singapore to acquire Nvidia chips, including founding a Chinese company called Shanghai Century Litong. Founded in 2023, it became an Nvidia-preferred cloud partner, giving it priority access to chips, The Information reported . The Information also reported that Shanghai Century Litong facilitated buying $7.5 billion worth of Nvidia’s chips, including banned chips. Nvidia’s head lawyer, Tim Teter, intervened in a 2025 U.S. government probe surrounding the suspected smuggling of AI chips by Megaspeed International, Bloomberg reported . Teter contacted Commerce Under Secretary Jeffrey Kessler asking questions about whether the Trump administration played a role in detaining Alice Huang. In early 2025, Alice Huang and a business partner sought China-based investors for an Asian data center, promising they had no problem in securing GPUs, the Financial Times reported. On Sunday night, President Trump weighed in on Huang’s controversy and showed support for the Nvidia CEO. “I have not spoken to him about it. I just know he’s a fine person, but you never know what’s going on,” Trump said. When asked if Huang should remain chief of Nvidia , Trump said, “I think so. Oh yeah, sure.” Jensen Huang wrote in a letter to Nvidia employees — which was also published as a press release — that he cheated on his wife. “I owe my family and all of you an apology,” Huang told his company. “I was unfaithful to my wife. My actions hurt her and our children. There is no excuse for what I did. I am deeply sorry.” Huang did not mention Alice Huang by name in the message, but linked his infidelity to “the national security concerns raised in news reports.” “Nvidia’s Board of Directors has initiated an independent investigation. I support the investigation and will cooperate fully. I love our country and our company. I am committed to protecting Nvidia and supporting America’s national security. I am proud and grateful to be an American,” Huang wrote. Nvidia shares slid over 5% the following day. An Nvidia spokesperson denied that this relationship was something out of the ordinary. “Jensen’s interactions with Ms. Huang are not unusual or unexpected. Meetings with customers are part of a CEO’s job; Jensen talks with thousands of customer executives every year,” Nvidia spokesperson John Rizzo said. He added that “if the U.S. government believes that any person is a threat to American industry, it would let us know.” U.S. officials circulated a secret memo among policymakers that warned that Megaspeed’s Alice Huang, who had a relationship with Jensen Huang, was a spy for China’s Ministry of State Security. This memo was not public knowledge until it was later reported by the New York Times. Secretary of State Marco Rubio supervised the drafting of the memo. Around the same time, per the New York Times’ report , U.S. President Donald Trump was briefed about intelligence findings that possible Chinese spy Alice Huang had formed a close relationship with Jensen Huang. Trump did not act on this information. The Nvidia CEO, an ally of Trump , has repeatedly advocated for the U.S. government to let Nvidia expand its business in China. Megaspeed, a neocloud that used Nvidia chips, had been renting computing power to Chinese internet giant Alibaba and other Chinese companies, the Times reported. A Commerce Department official who had visited Megaspeed’s data center in Malaysia in 2024 had found a hoard of Nvidia equipment that was still packed in boxes and the concern was that this equipment was being directly shipped somewhere else, like China, rather than installed and sold as a cloud service. Jensen Huang had been spotted socializing with Megaspeed executive Alice Huang as early as 2024 in Taiwan, where the Nvidia CEO was born. These investigations into Megaspeed highlighted concerns about the degree to which Nvidia is able to track its chip exports. At the time, an Nvidia spokesperson told press that the company did not have “any reason to believe products had been diverted.” Anthropic launches Claude Meetings to turn workplace discussions into plans and tasks Aisha Malik Jensen Huang’s alleged honeypot scandal has inspired some top-notch memes Dominic-Madori Davis Lucas Ropek Waymo robotaxis kept illegally passing school buses after software fix, feds say Kirsten Korosec

coreStoryFacts.text: U.S. officials circulated a secret memo among policymakers that warned that Megaspeed’s Alice Huang, who had a relationship with Jensen Huang, was a spy for China’s Ministry of State Security.
This memo was not public knowledge until it was later reported by the New York Times.
Jensen Huang wrote in a letter to Nvidia employees — which was also published as a press release — that he cheated on his wife.
The story took a sudden new turn on Wednesday.

Citing five people who worked at Nvidia, the Times reported that Huang also had an extramarital relationship with Kimberly Powell, the company’s vice president of health care, who reports directly to him.
Nvidia, Huang and Powell have not confirmed the report.
Reached by a Times reporter, Huang reportedly said, “I don’t think you should be talking to me directly,” before hanging up.
Huang famously delegates very little and has about 60 direct reports, he has said .
As the controversy unfolds, we are organizing the most relevant events into a reverse-chronological timeline to keep you up to date.

The chairmen of the House Select Committee on China, the House Foreign Affairs Committee, and the House Intelligence Committee formally requested a closed-door briefing from Jensen Huang, with the request reported around November 5, 2026.
No public response from Huang or Nvidia was identified in the cited reporting at that time.
During 2024 and into 2025 , media reports said Jensen Huang and Alice Huang were photographed or observed socializing in Taiwan, where Jensen Huang was born.
The memo allegedly stated she had been recruited to gather information about Jensen Huang .
It also alleged she was tasked with influencing Nvidia’s commercial position on advanced chip sales to China.
Jensen Huang co-founded Nvidia in 1993 and has led it since.
Alice Huang , also known as Huang Le, is a Chinese citizen and former senior executive at Megaspeed, a Singapore-based data-center company that rents computing capacity built on Nvidia processors.
Nvidia responded by characterizing Jensen Huang’s interactions with her as ordinary customer-related contact.

Public reporting has not established what information Alice Huang allegedly obtained, whether any Nvidia proprietary information was transferred, or whether export-control violations involving Megaspeed occurred.

Congressional committees have requested access to Jensen Huang ; no hearing date has been announced, and until investigators publish conclusions or authorities bring formal charges, the espionage allegations remain unproven.

In October 2025 , U.S. and Singapore authorities reportedly examined whether Megaspeed had helped Chinese firms, including Alibaba, obtain Nvidia processors in potential violation of U.S. export restrictions.

Nvidia’s board has opened an independent investigation into its founder and CEO, Jensen Huang , after he admitted to an affair with a woman that US media report was a Chinese intelligence asset. The claims first surfaced in a New York Times report on October 29. They are unproven publicly, China rejects them, and Nvidia says nothing suggests its secrets were compromised. The story stretches back more than two years, to a US probe of one of Nvidia’s customers. It also lands as Nvidia leans harder into Europe: on October 13, Huang said in Paris that it would announce $2 billion in new European AI deals. Alice Huang, also reported as Huang Le, worked as an executive at Megaspeed. The Times reported that US officials believe she was an asset of China’s Ministry of State Security. The Financial Times reported that officials believed her task was to gather information on Huang, including by pushing him to argue for looser limits on chip exports to China. She has no relation to Jensen Huang. She has not commented publicly, and the FT said it could not reach her. Megaspeed was spun out of a Chinese gaming company in 2023. Trade data cited by the Times indicates that a Malaysia-linked company associated with Megaspeed bought at least $4.8 billion of Nvidia equipment between June 2024 and February 2026. Megaspeed has faced questions over whether chips were diverted to China. Nvidia says those claims were “thoroughly investigated and debunked” last year. “We trust that if we were the target of a genuine threat, the U.S. government would have notified us,” Nvidia spokesperson John Rizzo said. Huang wrote to staff: “I was unfaithful to my wife. My actions hurt her and our children. There is no excuse for what I did. I am deeply sorry.” He did not name the woman and said he would cooperate with the inquiry. Nvidia’s board said a committee of independent directors, assisted by outside counsel, will run it, and that it had “no reason to believe” national security or Nvidia secrets were compromised. Secretary of State Marco Rubio called the matter an “internal corporate matter.” One point is settled: Huang has confirmed the affair. The spying claims rest on reports citing US officials, and nothing public shows that Nvidia’s confidential information was compromised. Huang spent much of October pitching Europe. Nvidia puts its total European commitment at close to $10 billion and does not split it between equity stakes and infrastructure. In the same Paris speech, it flagged planned minority stakes in four French startups: Doctolib, Genesis AI, Pigment and Entalpic. Amounts were not disclosed. Nvidia’s European footprint goes well beyond those four. Trending Topics counted 26 European tech companies Nvidia has backed over three years, including Mistral AI, Wayve, Black Forest Labs, Nscale and ElevenLabs, plus 13 newly announced stakes. By the publication’s own extrapolation from PitchBook data, Nvidia’s commitments equal roughly a tenth of European tech venture funding in 2026, though check sizes are rarely disclosed. For European founders and investors, the worry is simple. A leadership crisis could slow Nvidia’s dealmaking, and tighter US scrutiny of its China ties could change how European governments see the company. The House chairs asked Huang to confirm by November 11 whether he will brief the committees on November 18, one day after Nvidia’s quarterly earnings. The board inquiry has no announced end date, and Washington has given no public sign of how the FBI’s interest affects Huang or Nvidia. Huang is one of AI’s best-known figures and has argued for keeping some chip sales to China open. The FT reported that he lobbied Trump earlier this year to allow exports of Nvidia’s H200 chip. The allegations could strengthen calls for tighter export controls and raise governance questions at a company closely tied to its CEO. Analyst Dan Ives expects Huang to stay for now but warned of a risk he could be removed, depending on what the board finds. Nvidia is also pushing into AI financing, including agreements with six asset managers to mobilise more than $500 billion in third-party capital for AI infrastructure . TFN has also covered Nvidia’s position in the AI chip market and how its dominance is being challenged. If the inquiry clears Huang, does Nvidia’s China exposure still leave it vulnerable in Washington? extraction.body: Russia has cleared domestic exchanges to begin cryptocurrency trading from Nov. 22, 2026, subject to approval of their trading rules by the Bank of Russia. Russia has allowed domestic exchanges to begin cryptocurrency trading from Nov. 22, provided their trading rules receive approval from the Bank of Russia. Exchanges must register market participants, maintain records of orders and transactions, calculate pricing indicators and report trading activity to the central bank. The new requirements follow Russia's September cryptocurrency legislation, which established a regulated framework for exchanges, brokers, crypto exchange providers and digital depositories. Moscow Exchange plans to launch cryptocurrency trading on Dec. 11 report from Interfax, the Russian Ministry of Justice has registered a central bank directive setting out the requirements for organized trading in cryptocurrencies and digital rights. The directive allows exchanges to introduce cryptocurrency trading through the country's existing financial market infrastructure, provided their operating rules have been agreed upon with the regulator. 22 effective date comes ahead of Moscow Exchange's planned Dec. 1 launch, when the country's largest securities trading platform expects to begin offering Bitcoin, Ether, and USDT transactions. Russian crypto exchanges must meet new trading requirements Before launching cryptocurrency trading, exchanges must establish procedures for registering market participants, maintaining transaction records, and monitoring trading activity. The requirements cover brokers, trust managers, and central counterparties involved in cryptocurrency transactions. Trading organizers must maintain separate registers of orders and completed trades, giving regulators access to records of market activity. Exchanges will be responsible for calculating several pricing indicators, including current prices, weighted average prices, market prices, and closing prices. The Bank of Russia has required trading platforms to submit information about ongoing trading activity and completed transactions through the same reporting procedures currently used for other financial instruments. The regulator had outlined similar requirements in July when it published its initial cryptocurrency market regulations, which covered organized trading, price calculations, and digital depository operations. The framework places cryptocurrency trading within the reporting and market supervision arrangements already used by regulated Russian exchanges. Bitcoin, Ether, and USDT approved for retail investors Russia's latest exchange trading rules follow a separate regulatory decision on Nov. 6 that approved Bitcoin, Ether, and Tether's USDT for purchase by nonqualified investors. The Bank of Russia confirmed that the approved asset list would take effect on Nov. 17, allowing exchanges to admit those cryptocurrencies for public trading from that date. Transactions can take place through brokers, trust managers, and registered cryptocurrency exchange providers. Qualified investors face no equivalent purchase limit and can access other cryptocurrencies, although both investor categories must pass a knowledge test and review the associated investment risks before trading. The central bank selected eligible retail cryptocurrencies using market capitalization, average daily trading volume, and pricing records from foreign exchanges spanning at least five years. Russia's regulated cryptocurrency market opened on Sept. As previously reported by crypto.news, the legislation established separate roles for existing financial institutions, cryptocurrency exchange providers, and digital depositories responsible for recording ownership and transfers. Moscow Exchange prepares for December launch Moscow Exchange has scheduled its cryptocurrency trading launch for Dec. Boris Blokhin, senior managing director for sales and business development at Moscow Exchange, said in October that the platform would use a partner settlement digital depository where participating firms would open accounts. The exchange expects to operate under its existing regulatory permissions without obtaining additional licenses specifically for cryptocurrency trading. Its planned trading service will support Bitcoin, Ether, and USDT, with trading hours expected to run from 6:50 a.m. to 11:50 p.m. Brokers will provide investor access to the platform, while the partner digital depository will handle the custody and settlement arrangements for cryptocurrency transactions. Russia has already begun registering the institutions needed to support the new market. The Bank of Russia said on November 11 that exchanges may begin organized cryptocurrency trading on November 22, 2026, after securing approval for their trading rules. The Russia Bitcoin trading framework brings BTC ▲ $73,812.00 into the country’s supervised financial markets, while Moscow Exchange still targets December 1 for its launch.
The opening comes with restrictions: ordinary investors face an annual purchase limit through each intermediary, and Russia’s largest exchange and its clearing house remain under US sanctions.

The central bank’s ordinance allows exchanges to introduce organized cryptocurrency trading from November 22 , provided they first agree on their operating rules with the regulator. That approval is a condition for opening a market, rather than an automatic consequence of the effective date.

Trading venues must register participating brokers, trust managers and central counterparties. They must also maintain registers of orders and completed deals, monitor activity and send trading information to the Bank of Russia.

Price calculations form another part of the requirements. Exchanges must calculate current, weighted-average, market and closing prices, giving the regulator a set of pricing measures alongside the transaction records.

Market participants should remain vigilant regarding potential updates from the Central Bank as the implementation date nears. Russia has allowed domestic exchanges to begin cryptocurrency trading from Nov. 22, provided their trading rules receive approval from the Bank of Russia. Exchanges must register market participants, maintain records of orders and transactions, calculate pricing indicators and report trading activity to the central bank. The new requirements follow Russia's September cryptocurrency legislation, which established a regulated framework for exchanges, brokers, crypto exchange providers and digital depositories. Moscow Exchange plans to launch cryptocurrency trading on Dec. 11 report from Interfax, the Russian Ministry of Justice has registered a central bank directive setting out the requirements for organized trading in cryptocurrencies and digital rights. The directive allows exchanges to introduce cryptocurrency trading through the country's existing financial market infrastructure, provided their operating rules have been agreed upon with the regulator. 22 effective date comes ahead of Moscow Exchange's planned Dec. 1 launch, when the country's largest securities trading platform expects to begin offering Bitcoin, Ether, and USDT transactions. Russian crypto exchanges must meet new trading requirements Before launching cryptocurrency trading, exchanges must establish procedures for registering market participants, maintaining transaction records, and monitoring trading activity. The requirements cover brokers, trust managers, and central counterparties involved in cryptocurrency transactions. Trading organizers must maintain separate registers of orders and completed trades, giving regulators access to records of market activity. Exchanges will be responsible for calculating several pricing indicators, including current prices, weighted average prices, market prices, and closing prices. The Bank of Russia has required trading platforms to submit information about ongoing trading activity and completed transactions through the same reporting procedures currently used for other financial instruments. The regulator had outlined similar requirements in July when it published its initial cryptocurrency market regulations, which covered organized trading, price calculations, and digital depository operations. The framework places cryptocurrency trading within the reporting and market supervision arrangements already used by regulated Russian exchanges. Bitcoin, Ether, and USDT approved for retail investors Russia's latest exchange trading rules follow a separate regulatory decision on Nov. 6 that approved Bitcoin, Ether, and Tether's USDT for purchase by nonqualified investors. The Bank of Russia confirmed that the approved asset list would take effect on Nov. 17, allowing exchanges to admit those cryptocurrencies for public trading from that date. Transactions can take place through brokers, trust managers, and registered cryptocurrency exchange providers. Qualified investors face no equivalent purchase limit and can access other cryptocurrencies, although both investor categories must pass a knowledge test and review the associated investment risks before trading. The central bank selected eligible retail cryptocurrencies using market capitalization, average daily trading volume, and pricing records from foreign exchanges spanning at least five years. Russia's regulated cryptocurrency market opened on Sept. As previously reported by crypto.news, the legislation established separate roles for existing financial institutions, cryptocurrency exchange providers, and digital depositories responsible for recording ownership and transfers. Boris Blokhin, senior managing director for sales and business development at Moscow Exchange, said in October that the platform would use a partner settlement digital depository where participating firms would open accounts. The exchange expects to operate under its existing regulatory permissions without obtaining additional licenses specifically for cryptocurrency trading. Its planned trading service will support Bitcoin, Ether, and USDT, with trading hours expected to run from 6:50 a.m. to 11:50 p.m. Brokers will provide investor access to the platform, while the partner digital depository will handle the custody and settlement arrangements for cryptocurrency transactions. Russia has already begun registering the institutions needed to support the new market. In October, the central bank approved its first operators, initially admitting four cryptocurrency exchange providers and five digital depositories. According to the central bank's October announcement, registered digital depositories can record and transfer cryptocurrencies and digital rights, while cryptocurrency exchange providers can buy and sell digital currencies on their own behalf outside organized trading. The registered institutions must comply with applicable transaction and recordkeeping requirements and bring their operations fully into line with the new legislation by Sept.

The Bank of Russia said on November 11 that exchanges may begin organized cryptocurrency trading on November 22, 2026, after securing approval for their trading rules. The Russia Bitcoin trading framework brings BTC ▲ $73,812.00 into the country’s supervised financial markets, while Moscow Exchange still targets December 1 for its launch.
The opening comes with restrictions: ordinary investors face an annual purchase limit through each intermediary, and Russia’s largest exchange and its clearing house remain under US sanctions.

The central bank’s ordinance allows exchanges to introduce organized cryptocurrency trading from November 22 , provided they first agree on their operating rules with the regulator. That approval is a condition for opening a market, rather than an automatic consequence of the effective date.

The Justice Ministry registered the ordinance on November 3, and the regulator published it on November 11. It amends the rules governing organized trading, bringing cryptocurrency transactions into the reporting arrangements already used for other assets.

Trading venues must register participating brokers, trust managers and central counterparties. They must also maintain registers of orders and completed deals, monitor activity and send trading information to the Bank of Russia.

Price calculations form another part of the requirements. Exchanges must calculate current, weighted-average, market and closing prices, giving the regulator a set of pricing measures alongside the transaction records.

Moscow Exchange, Russia’s largest trading venue, announced on November 2 that it plans to introduce Bitcoin, Ether and USDT ▼ $0.9991 transactions on December 1. The initial rollout is planned as a pilot while participating firms connect to the service.

The exchange intends to use its existing stock-market systems. Its proposed cryptocurrency session runs from 6:50 a.m. to 11:50 p.m. Moscow time, with clients able to settle transactions on the same day or the following day.

Brokers will provide investor access, while the National Clearing Centre is expected to clear Moscow Exchange’s cryptocurrency deals. A partner settlement digital depository is planned to handle custody and settlement arrangements, with participating firms opening accounts there.

Boris Blokhin, a senior managing director at Moscow Exchange, said in October that the venue expected to operate under its existing permissions without additional licenses. The November ordinance separately requires agreement with the central bank on the rules governing cryptocurrency trading itself.

In January 2022, the Bank of Russia proposed banning cryptocurrency exchanges. It now oversees their entry into a licensed market under Federal Law No. 282-FZ, “On Digital Currencies and Digital Rights,” whose main provisions took effect on September 1.

The law recognizes cryptocurrency as property and establishes licensed roles for exchanges, brokers, managers, depositories and exchange providers. It also opens a supervised channel for cross-border trade, while retaining the prohibition on using cryptocurrency to pay for goods and services inside Russia.

However, the requirement for compliance and oversight may also pose challenges for smaller exchanges that lack the infrastructure to meet regulatory demands. Market participants should remain vigilant regarding potential updates from the Central Bank as the implementation date nears. sources.body: I never liked hunting for Golden Skulltulas in The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time.

extraction.body: I never liked hunting for Golden Skulltulas in The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time. The game has 100 of them tucked all over Hyrule, and even over my many hours with the N64 classic growing up, I can’t remember ever actually finding all of them, or even wanting to. Jumping into the Ocarina of Time remake, I expected to ignore the Golden Skulltulas once again. But while poking around Nintendo’s Zelda Notes companion app, I discovered that its maps are a huge help to tracking down all of the elusive golden spiders — and pretty much every other collectible in the game — and now I find myself constantly opening up the app to make sure I haven’t missed a secret. Inside Zelda Notes, which is available in the free Nintendo Switch app (you don’t need a Switch Online subscription to use it), you can peruse a big map of Hyrule and tap on individual areas for a closer look. While exploring, I’ll often come across the telltale Golden Skulltula sound but have no idea how to get to the tricky spider, even with the help of additional chimes from the new Echo Gem Skulltula tracking item. But with a peek at the Zelda Notes app, I can pinpoint the exact location of where the Skulltula is supposed to be and if I need to use a certain item or change the time of day to be able to get to it. I recently delved into the Shadow Temple, for example, and I couldn’t figure out how to get up to a Skulltula that I saw while coming down an elevator. But when I checked the icon on the Zelda Notes map, it said that I needed the Scarecrow Song to create a hookshot point, which I hadn’t gotten yet. Zelda Notes has been useful for tracking down Pieces of Heart, too, which give Link more health once you collect enough. While running up and down Zora’s River, I kept seeing two Pieces of Heart on faraway ledges that I couldn’t figure out how to get to. (My memories of my extensive time with Ocarina of Time as a kid also failed me.) But tapping one of the icons on the Zelda Notes map revealed that I needed a Cucco to get to it — and suddenly, I understood why there was one of the chirping white birds near the entrance of the zone. Yes, it can be annoying to have to open my phone and dig through an app to track down all of the Skulltulas and other objects of curiosity scattered around Hyrule. And sure, I could just look up an online guide, but that often means wading through walkthroughs of varying quality, trusting an AI summary, or scrubbing through a YouTube video. But with Zelda Notes, I’m usually in and out relatively quickly, putting down my phone after seeing a clue or an icon that pushes me in the direction of the next golden spider. I’ve already found more than 70 Golden Skulltulas, and to my surprise, I now want to hunt for the full 100.

While running up and down Zora’s River, I kept seeing two Pieces of Heart on faraway ledges that I couldn’t figure out how to get to. (My memories of my extensive time with Ocarina of Time as a kid also failed me.) But tapping one of the icons on the Zelda Notes map revealed that I needed a Cucco to get to it — and suddenly, I understood why there was one of the chirping white birds near the entrance of the zone.
Yes, it can be annoying to have to open my phone and dig through an app to track down all of the Skulltulas and other objects of curiosity scattered around Hyrule.
And sure, I could just look up an online guide, but that often means wading through walkthroughs of varying quality, trusting an AI summary, or scrubbing through a YouTube video.
But with Zelda Notes, I’m usually in and out relatively quickly, putting down my phone after seeing a clue or an icon that pushes me in the direction of the next golden spider.
I’ve already found more than 70 Golden Skulltulas, and to my surprise, I now want to hunt for the full 100.

extraction.body: The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time hit Switch 2 today, and, as Kyle Hilliard pointed out in our review , it is pretty excellent. Along with its remarkable visual upgrade, the new Switch 2 remake of Ocarina of Time adds quality-of-life improvements and modernizes the control scheme. As part of that, Nintendo has added the ability to jump and sprint. While that works well to make the game feel new, I quickly realized it sometimes clashes with another new improvement: a free camera controlled by the right stick. Holding down the sprint button to get through areas as fast as possible can make it tricky to keep the camera where you want it, but thankfully, if you have the Switch 2 Pro Controller, there's an easy fix. After hours of running around, I was awestruck by the level of detail and updates, but I found myself constantly fighting with the camera, or at the very least, needing to take a strange claw-style grip to be able to direct the camera with the right stick, while holding down the A button to sprint. If you're a casual Switch 2 player, you might not have even noticed the back buttons on the Pro Controller, or you just have no idea what they do. Those buttons can be remapped on a per-game basis and it's a simple process. Everyone has their own preferences, but, for example, for high-mobility shooters, I like remapping one of those to reload and one to jump. I've never felt the need to remap in a Zelda game, but after feeling the need to do so with The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time on Switch 2, I might do so going forward. If you, like me, struggle to comfortably steer the new free camera while running through hallways, towns, dungeons, and, yes, Hyrule Field, you might want to consider remapping your controller. As you can see in the above image, the placement of Jump and Dash on the face buttons can make it difficult to simultaneously control the camera and sprint. This isn't typically a problem in most modern games, as clicking the right stick is often a toggle to sprint, but in The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time for Switch 2, you need to hold the button. If you have the Nintendo Switch 2 Pro Controller, copying one button's functionality to the buttons on the back of the controller is simple. All you need to do is hold the Home button on the Switch 2 Pro Controller for a moment until the Switch 2 system menu appears on the right side. Along with Power Options and any Bluetooth audio devices you have available, there is also the option to map GL and GR, the controller's back buttons on the left and right, respectively. Navigate down the menu to the GL and GR, then select which one you'd like to map. It will ask you which button you want to assign to the one you selected. Everyone can choose whatever makes sense in their own head, but mapping A (Roll and Dash) to GL and X (Jump) to GR made the most sense to me. Now, while I'm using the Switch 2 Pro Controller, I can use my middle finger to hold the GL button to Dash around without removing my thumb from the camera-controlling right stick. And the best part is that, since you're not removing the functionality of the A or X buttons, you can still use them when it makes sense. For example, A also controls actions like opening up a treasure chest or door, and in my head, that feels like a face-button action, whereas rolling and dashing feel right mapped to the back buttons. The only downside is that, since this functionality is new for Switch 2 Pro Controllers, it isn't available if you're using the Joy-Cons or a Switch 1 Pro Controller. Also, it can make switching over to handheld mode challenging, as you don't have access to the back buttons in that play style. © 1991 to Game Informer. All Rights Reserved.

sources.title: I just played The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time remake — and it looks and plays better than I could have ever imagined - Tom's Guide
passages: It’s funny to think that playing the Ocarina of Time remake now has me excited to jump back into the original, so I have even more of a memorized reference guide to go to once this Switch 2 exclusive arrives on November 5, 2026.
I couldn’t help but crack a nostalgic smile at the sight of that dancing couple near the watering hole, who looked expectedly better than their N64 and 3DS variations.
The use of loading screens between the town’s many areas wasn’t much of a bother, even though I’d prefer it if there were seamless navigation in this remake.
And after making my way through three sections of the game, I walked away with even more anticipation for its November release.
At one point, I finally abandoned my fanboyish ways and tried the N64 at my best friend’s house.
One of the first games I played was The Legend of Zelda: Majora’s Mask.
I know that sounds insane—playing the second N64 adventure in Link’s famed series before the first one, which is regarded as the GOAT, is wild.
Elton Jones covers AI for Tom’s Guide, and tests all the latest models, from ChatGPT to Gemini to Claude to see which tools perform best — and how they can improve everyday productivity.

While I didn’t have enough time to solve all of Forest Temple’s puzzles and clash with Phantom Ganon, I got more than enough of a sense of just how much better this area looks and sounds in its remade form.
But seeing Young Link and his fellow forest denizens in motion convinced me that the remake’s visual presentation looks pretty damned good.

My grade school lunch breaks and recess sessions were filled with passionate debates about Crash Bandicoot vs. Super Mario 64, why the PS1 is the ultimate RPG console while the N64 isn’t and how Nintendo’s 3D console was the king of wrestling games (unlike the PS1). At one point, I finally abandoned my fanboyish ways and tried the N64 at my best friend’s house. One of the first games I played was The Legend of Zelda: Majora’s Mask. I know that sounds insane—playing the second N64 adventure in Link’s famed series before the first one, which is regarded as the GOAT, is wild. What’s even crazier is that I didn't play The Ocarina of Time until this year, through the Nintendo Switch Online + Expansion Pack . After making my way through Hyrule Field and Kakariko Village, I finally realized all the hype about the quintessential action/adventure game was well warranted. With fresh memories of the original swirling around in my head, I went into the Switch 2 remake of Ocarina of Time with extremely high expectations. And after making my way through three sections of the game, I walked away with even more anticipation for its November release. The start of my foray into Link’s remade adventure kicked off with me helping Link search for his first sword and shield. As I ran (and jumped!) around Kokiri Forest, I compared the graphical presentation of the remake to the N64 original and even the 3DS version. The porcelain doll look of Link and the rest of the Kokiri people felt a bit off to me at first when I watched the initial reveal trailer for this remake. But seeing Young Link and his fellow forest denizens in motion convinced me that the remake’s visual presentation looks pretty damned good. The forest’s more detailed woodland locales are equally impressive, as are the inner sanctums of the village’s populace. Get instant access to breaking news, the hottest reviews, great deals and helpful tips. Watching the initial cutscene unfold where Navi navigates toward Link’s hut is a bit different this time around, as the first-person viewpoint gets switched to a third-person one. I have no qualms about that one bit, especially cause the instance of Navi flying into a gate comes off a little bit more humorous with that viewpoint switch up (no pun intended). All the familiarities of this section, such as dodging that massive boulder to pick up the Kokiri Sword and buying the Deku Shield he needs to get past Mido, are intact as expected. And thankfully, the spruced-up visuals do enough to make those nostalgic activities feel a bit fresh while retaining what made them so endearing in the first place. Once I made my way out into the iconic Hyrule Field, I couldn’t help but be taken aback by just how much more expressive it looked this time around. Fully detailed shrubs of grass, the presence of a noticeable mist floating through the air, patches of colorful flowers, towering trees and dirt roads make up the entirety of this remake’s newly realized pasture. The same feelings of excitement and amazement remained intact once I finally entered Hyrule Castle Town. I couldn’t help but crack a nostalgic smile at the sight of that dancing couple near the watering hole, who looked expectedly better than their N64 and 3DS variations. The use of loading screens between the town’s many areas wasn’t much of a bother, even though I’d prefer it if there were seamless navigation in this remake. Hyrule Castle Town’s vibrancy is on full display and is proof of just how jaw-dropping this new version of Ocarina of Time truly is. I’m sure I’ll spend a few moments watching the NPCs move through their daily routines, chat with them to see what new bits of dialogue they may have and roll & jump around every corner of their wholesome town once I get the full game in my hands. The furthest I made it into the OG version of Ocarina of Time thus far is the famed “Forest Temple,” so I was pretty hyped to find out I’d be getting the chance to hop into its remade rendition. I was surprised by just how amazing it looked on the inside and outside. Coming to blows with rabid Wolfos, using Link’s trusty Hookshot to knock Blue Bubbles out of the air and carefully picking my spots to do damage on Stalfos soldiers felt good from a combat standpoint. Landing precise sword swings, blocking and flinging bombs brought with it a nice sense of impact, which appeals to someone like me who’s big on action games that deliver an appropriate sense of combat feedback. I spammed Link’s spinning sword attack far too many times than I can count, which is proof of just how much more I liked smacking around his foes in this remake compared to the original. Running through the Forest Temple showcased a much moodier atmosphere, thanks to the remake’s darker lighting. That brooding feeling I couldn’t shake was even more apparent once I ran through the temple’s signature twisting hallway, which led to another moment where I was more than impressed with the remake’s visual flair. While I didn’t have enough time to solve all of Forest Temple’s puzzles and clash with Phantom Ganon, I got more than enough of a sense of just how much better this area looks and sounds in its remade form. It’s funny to think that playing the Ocarina of Time remake now has me excited to jump back into the original, so I have even more of a memorized reference guide to go to once this Switch 2 exclusive arrives on November 5, 2026. I have a few weeks to get it done so I can hop right into one of the most anticipated video game remakes ever made. The porcelain doll-like characters, revised musical arrangements, eye-popping graphical presentation and impactful combat all came together during my demo time to convince me Nintendo has something special in its hands that I can’t wait for you all to experience for yourselves. At one point, I finally abandoned my fanboyish ways and tried the N64 at my best friend’s house. One of the first games I played was The Legend of Zelda: Majora’s Mask.

I know that sounds insane—playing the second N64 adventure in Link’s famed series before the first one, which is regarded as the GOAT, is wild. What’s even crazier is that I didn't play The Ocarina of Time until this year, through the Nintendo Switch Online + Expansion Pack . After making my way through Hyrule Field and Kakariko Village, I finally realized all the hype about the quintessential action/adventure game was well warranted.

With fresh memories of the original swirling around in my head, I went into the Switch 2 remake of Ocarina of Time with extremely high expectations. And after making my way through three sections of the game, I walked away with even more anticipation for its November release.
The start of my foray into Link’s remade adventure kicked off with me helping Link search for his first sword and shield.

As I ran (and jumped!) around Kokiri Forest, I compared the graphical presentation of the remake to the N64 original and even the 3DS version. The porcelain doll look of Link and the rest of the Kokiri people felt a bit off to me at first when I watched the initial reveal trailer for this remake. All the familiarities of this section, such as dodging that massive boulder to pick up the Kokiri Sword and buying the Deku Shield he needs to get past Mido, are intact as expected.
And thankfully, the spruced-up visuals do enough to make those nostalgic activities feel a bit fresh while retaining what made them so endearing in the first place.

Fully detailed shrubs of grass, the presence of a noticeable mist floating through the air, patches of colorful flowers, towering trees and dirt roads make up the entirety of this remake’s newly realized pasture.
The same feelings of excitement and amazement remained intact once I finally entered Hyrule Castle Town.

It’s funny to think that playing the Ocarina of Time remake now has me excited to jump back into the original, so I have even more of a memorized reference guide to go to once this Switch 2 exclusive arrives on November 5, 2026.

extraction.body: The original The Legend of Zelda : Ocarina of Time has been certified as the highest-rated video game ever for a long time now. 2026’s Remake , however, has immediately climbed the charts and is currently this year’s top-rated title. The question then becomes, “Which one is actually better overall?” For my personal two cents, I still give the OG a slight edge. At the same time, that doesn’t take anything away from the Remake. In fact, 2026’s version of Ocarina is actually better in some cases. Let’s take a look at ten different ways Nintendo was able to take the classic and somehow improve on some aspects. Most obviously, the graphical and performance upgrades in OOT Remake are substantial. This isn’t a surprise at all since the OG is from the ’90s, but Remake still smashed it out of the park in terms of design and tone as well. Despite some concerns over glossy character models during the pre-launch phase of the game, the new art direction is constantly breathtaking and pulled off masterfully. Standouts are Lake Hylia with its gorgeous water effects, and Ganondorf’s Castle, which straight up looks like it’s ripped out of Mordor in Lord of the Rings. The hardest thing about going back for the original version of OOT is the control scheme and camera. Sure, the visuals are dated, but there’s a definite charm and style to them as well. The controls are just… old. This barrier to entry being removed in Zelda: Ocarina Remake was crucial to it succeeding in modern times. Thankfully, the right-stick camera works beautifully (though Z-Target centering was still kept in as well). Sword combat and shield blocking are fluid and snappy. Perhaps most importantly, however, is that projectile aiming can now be toggled between standard camera control and inverted. The 1998 game only offered inverted aiming, which is a total no-go for many modern gamers. There’s a certain charm in figuring out the auto-ledge jumping in N64 Ocarina, but it’s no surprise that having an actual, dedicated jump button in Remake is a massive improvement. Back in the day, Link’s jumping mechanics were the best Nintendo could muster, and we learned to adapt to them. But in 2026, not having an actual jump would’ve been a crime. This new ability also leads to some fun location and dungeon redesigns since Link can reach higher ledges and areas than ever before. A lot of players hopping into Remake (myself included) know almost everything about the N64 game. When picking up Remake, I wondered just how 1:1 everything would be, including things like gold skulltulas and room layouts. To my surprise, it was a blast to explore the new game and learn that many locations had been shuffled around or changed entirely. And this isn’t just a “better” change because it’s different. Instead, there are now several examples of things being placed more thoughtfully and satisfyingly in the game world. Take, for example, the Kokiri Sword, which now takes a little more parkour action to collect. I may know the lore and story of Zelda: Ocarina of Time better than any other video game. Upon recently replaying the OG, however, it’s funny how much of the narrative is a little bit underexplained. Case in point: the Triforce itself is shoddily explained, making it less impactful when considering why everyone seems to care so much about it. In Remake, most characters have a plethora of added or tweaked dialogue. A lot of this added exposition serves the game extremely well, making the stakes clearer and even giving us additional lore and info along the way. I didn’t expect to learn even more about Hyrule and the plot of the game in 2026, but the Remake gave me the opportunity. Growing up, we’d often have to make up video game character voices in our heads. Fully voice-acted games weren’t the norm yet. Aside from Navi shouting her classic “Hey!” and “Listen!” lines, the rest of the OG cast was relegated to grunts, screams, laughs, and moans. Hearing immediate narration voice-over when booting up Remake is a trip. For the most part, I found all the actor choices on-point, too. My personal standout is the English dub for Kaepora Gaebora, the Guiding Owl, played by Frank Todaro. There were doubts that Zelda: Ocarina of Time’s legendary soundtrack could be improved, but it somehow was. Of course, this is in large part due to the songs now being fully orchestrated, which was not an option on the Nintendo 64. Still, it wouldn’t have been hard to mess this one up with how beloved 1998’s tunes still are to this day. Thankfully, the full orchestration is gorgeous, as the new, sweeping melodies pack home way more emotion than ever before. Special shout-out to Saria’s Song, which comes back several times in a surprising, haunting fashion. While I wouldn’t say every dungeon was improved in the Remake, several were still fundamentally made better. In general, they’re all a bit more straightforward, which is nice for first-time players who aren’t used to retro game design. At the same time, simpler isn’t always better. In the case of dungeons like the Water Temple and Jabu-Jabu’s Belly, however, streamlining was the move. The migraine-inducing original Water Temple is reworked just enough that it went from my least favorite in the OG, to possibly my actual favorite in Remake. Most, if not all, of the dungeons are essentially at least on par with the original versions. The handful that actually made things better then stand out that much more this time around. While there aren’t too many challenging boss or enemy encounters in Zelda: Ocarina of Time Remake, fighting everything is still more fun than ever. This is thanks to many tweaks to encounter structure and entire enemy movesets. For example, King Dodongo now summons baby Dodongos during phases of the boss fight. Twinrova has an additional, arena-spanning spin attack. It’s a blast to have to reconsider and relearn these fights (and also practice them in the added Hall of Fallen Foes mode). The best things here, however, are the standard enemy moveset tweaks. A lot of us have fought thousands of skulltulas, wolfos, and tektites. To see all these monsters throwing different moves out that are actively more fun to engage with is incredible. Finally, OOT Remake does a wonderful job of making locations like Hyrule Castle Town and Kakariko Village feel more alive and lived-in than ever. Since time can pass in towns now, we’re treated to the game’s NPCs being on actual schedules and routines that we can follow and learn. This makes everyone feel like that much more of a thought-out character in many cases. For example, Grog used to just sit under the tree in Kakariko at night in the N64 game, and we didn’t ever learn much about him. Now, we can follow him around town, observing him lurking behind walls, waiting for his dad to go home so he doesn’t have to cross paths with him. It’s things like this that make Zelda: Ocarina of Time Remake feel more alive than ever. How do you think the two games compare? Let us know in the Insider Gaming Discord server . coreStoryFacts.text: I never liked hunting for Golden Skulltulas in The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time.

After hours of running around, I was awestruck by the level of detail and updates, but I found myself constantly fighting with the camera, or at the very least, needing to take a strange claw-style grip to be able to direct the camera with the right stick, while holding down the A button to sprint.
If you're a casual Switch 2 player, you might not have even noticed the back buttons on the Pro Controller, or you just have no idea what they do.
Those buttons can be remapped on a per-game basis and it's a simple process.
Everyone has their own preferences, but, for example, for high-mobility shooters, I like remapping one of those to reload and one to jump.
I've never felt the need to remap in a Zelda game, but after feeling the need to do so with The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time on Switch 2, I might do so going forward.
As part of that, Nintendo has added the ability to jump and sprint.
And the best part is that, since you're not removing the functionality of the A or X buttons, you can still use them when it makes sense.
Navigate down the menu to the GL and GR, then select which one you'd like to map.
Everyone can choose whatever makes sense in their own head, but mapping A (Roll and Dash) to GL and X (Jump) to GR made the most sense to me.

extraction.body: I never liked hunting for Golden Skulltulas in The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time. The game has 100 of them tucked all over Hyrule, and even over my many hours with the N64 classic growing up, I can’t remember ever actually finding all of them, or even wanting to. Jumping into the Ocarina of Time remake, I expected to ignore the Golden Skulltulas once again. But while poking around Nintendo’s Zelda Notes companion app, I discovered that its maps are a huge help to tracking down all of the elusive golden spiders — and pretty much every other collectible in the game — and now I find myself constantly opening up the app to make sure I haven’t missed a secret. Inside Zelda Notes, which is available in the free Nintendo Switch app (you don’t need a Switch Online subscription to use it), you can peruse a big map of Hyrule and tap on individual areas for a closer look. While exploring, I’ll often come across the telltale Golden Skulltula sound but have no idea how to get to the tricky spider, even with the help of additional chimes from the new Echo Gem Skulltula tracking item. But with a peek at the Zelda Notes app, I can pinpoint the exact location of where the Skulltula is supposed to be and if I need to use a certain item or change the time of day to be able to get to it. I recently delved into the Shadow Temple, for example, and I couldn’t figure out how to get up to a Skulltula that I saw while coming down an elevator. But when I checked the icon on the Zelda Notes map, it said that I needed the Scarecrow Song to create a hookshot point, which I hadn’t gotten yet. Zelda Notes has been useful for tracking down Pieces of Heart, too, which give Link more health once you collect enough. While running up and down Zora’s River, I kept seeing two Pieces of Heart on faraway ledges that I couldn’t figure out how to get to. (My memories of my extensive time with Ocarina of Time as a kid also failed me.) But tapping one of the icons on the Zelda Notes map revealed that I needed a Cucco to get to it — and suddenly, I understood why there was one of the chirping white birds near the entrance of the zone. Yes, it can be annoying to have to open my phone and dig through an app to track down all of the Skulltulas and other objects of curiosity scattered around Hyrule. And sure, I could just look up an online guide, but that often means wading through walkthroughs of varying quality, trusting an AI summary, or scrubbing through a YouTube video. But with Zelda Notes, I’m usually in and out relatively quickly, putting down my phone after seeing a clue or an icon that pushes me in the direction of the next golden spider. I’ve already found more than 70 Golden Skulltulas, and to my surprise, I now want to hunt for the full 100.

extraction.body: The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time hit Switch 2 today, and, as Kyle Hilliard pointed out in our review , it is pretty excellent. Along with its remarkable visual upgrade, the new Switch 2 remake of Ocarina of Time adds quality-of-life improvements and modernizes the control scheme. As part of that, Nintendo has added the ability to jump and sprint. While that works well to make the game feel new, I quickly realized it sometimes clashes with another new improvement: a free camera controlled by the right stick. Holding down the sprint button to get through areas as fast as possible can make it tricky to keep the camera where you want it, but thankfully, if you have the Switch 2 Pro Controller, there's an easy fix. After hours of running around, I was awestruck by the level of detail and updates, but I found myself constantly fighting with the camera, or at the very least, needing to take a strange claw-style grip to be able to direct the camera with the right stick, while holding down the A button to sprint. If you're a casual Switch 2 player, you might not have even noticed the back buttons on the Pro Controller, or you just have no idea what they do. Those buttons can be remapped on a per-game basis and it's a simple process. Everyone has their own preferences, but, for example, for high-mobility shooters, I like remapping one of those to reload and one to jump. I've never felt the need to remap in a Zelda game, but after feeling the need to do so with The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time on Switch 2, I might do so going forward. If you, like me, struggle to comfortably steer the new free camera while running through hallways, towns, dungeons, and, yes, Hyrule Field, you might want to consider remapping your controller. As you can see in the above image, the placement of Jump and Dash on the face buttons can make it difficult to simultaneously control the camera and sprint. This isn't typically a problem in most modern games, as clicking the right stick is often a toggle to sprint, but in The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time for Switch 2, you need to hold the button. If you have the Nintendo Switch 2 Pro Controller, copying one button's functionality to the buttons on the back of the controller is simple. All you need to do is hold the Home button on the Switch 2 Pro Controller for a moment until the Switch 2 system menu appears on the right side. Along with Power Options and any Bluetooth audio devices you have available, there is also the option to map GL and GR, the controller's back buttons on the left and right, respectively. Navigate down the menu to the GL and GR, then select which one you'd like to map. It will ask you which button you want to assign to the one you selected. Everyone can choose whatever makes sense in their own head, but mapping A (Roll and Dash) to GL and X (Jump) to GR made the most sense to me. Now, while I'm using the Switch 2 Pro Controller, I can use my middle finger to hold the GL button to Dash around without removing my thumb from the camera-controlling right stick. And the best part is that, since you're not removing the functionality of the A or X buttons, you can still use them when it makes sense. For example, A also controls actions like opening up a treasure chest or door, and in my head, that feels like a face-button action, whereas rolling and dashing feel right mapped to the back buttons. The only downside is that, since this functionality is new for Switch 2 Pro Controllers, it isn't available if you're using the Joy-Cons or a Switch 1 Pro Controller. Also, it can make switching over to handheld mode challenging, as you don't have access to the back buttons in that play style. © 1991 to Game Informer. All Rights Reserved.

At one point, I finally abandoned my fanboyish ways and tried the N64 at my best friend’s house. One of the first games I played was The Legend of Zelda: Majora’s Mask.

I know that sounds insane—playing the second N64 adventure in Link’s famed series before the first one, which is regarded as the GOAT, is wild. What’s even crazier is that I didn't play The Ocarina of Time until this year, through the Nintendo Switch Online + Expansion Pack . After making my way through Hyrule Field and Kakariko Village, I finally realized all the hype about the quintessential action/adventure game was well warranted.

With fresh memories of the original swirling around in my head, I went into the Switch 2 remake of Ocarina of Time with extremely high expectations. And after making my way through three sections of the game, I walked away with even more anticipation for its November release.
The start of my foray into Link’s remade adventure kicked off with me helping Link search for his first sword and shield.

As I ran (and jumped!) around Kokiri Forest, I compared the graphical presentation of the remake to the N64 original and even the 3DS version. The porcelain doll look of Link and the rest of the Kokiri people felt a bit off to me at first when I watched the initial reveal trailer for this remake. But seeing Young Link and his fellow forest denizens in motion convinced me that the remake’s visual presentation looks pretty damned good. The forest’s more detailed woodland locales are equally impressive, as are the inner sanctums of the village’s populace.

All the familiarities of this section, such as dodging that massive boulder to pick up the Kokiri Sword and buying the Deku Shield he needs to get past Mido, are intact as expected.
And thankfully, the spruced-up visuals do enough to make those nostalgic activities feel a bit fresh while retaining what made them so endearing in the first place.
Once I made my way out into the iconic Hyrule Field, I couldn’t help but be taken aback by just how much more expressive it looked this time around.

Fully detailed shrubs of grass, the presence of a noticeable mist floating through the air, patches of colorful flowers, towering trees and dirt roads make up the entirety of this remake’s newly realized pasture.
The same feelings of excitement and amazement remained intact once I finally entered Hyrule Castle Town.

I couldn’t help but crack a nostalgic smile at the sight of that dancing couple near the watering hole, who looked expectedly better than their N64 and 3DS variations. The use of loading screens between the town’s many areas wasn’t much of a bother, even though I’d prefer it if there were seamless navigation in this remake. Hyrule Castle Town’s vibrancy is on full display and is proof of just how jaw-dropping this new version of Ocarina of Time truly is.

I’m sure I’ll spend a few moments watching the NPCs move through their daily routines, chat with them to see what new bits of dialogue they may have and roll & jump around every corner of their wholesome town once I get the full game in my hands.
The furthest I made it into the OG version of Ocarina of Time thus far is the famed “Forest Temple,” so I was pretty hyped to find out I’d be getting the chance to hop into its remade rendition.

I was surprised by just how amazing it looked on the inside and outside. Coming to blows with rabid Wolfos, using Link’s trusty Hookshot to knock Blue Bubbles out of the air and carefully picking my spots to do damage on Stalfos soldiers felt good from a combat standpoint.

Landing precise sword swings, blocking and flinging bombs brought with it a nice sense of impact, which appeals to someone like me who’s big on action games that deliver an appropriate sense of combat feedback. I spammed Link’s spinning sword attack far too many times than I can count, which is proof of just how much more I liked smacking around his foes in this remake compared to the original.

Running through the Forest Temple showcased a much moodier atmosphere, thanks to the remake’s darker lighting. That brooding feeling I couldn’t shake was even more apparent once I ran through the temple’s signature twisting hallway, which led to another moment where I was more than impressed with the remake’s visual flair.

While I didn’t have enough time to solve all of Forest Temple’s puzzles and clash with Phantom Ganon, I got more than enough of a sense of just how much better this area looks and sounds in its remade form.

It’s funny to think that playing the Ocarina of Time remake now has me excited to jump back into the original, so I have even more of a memorized reference guide to go to once this Switch 2 exclusive arrives on November 5, 2026.
I have a few weeks to get it done so I can hop right into one of the most anticipated video game remakes ever made.

The porcelain doll-like characters, revised musical arrangements, eye-popping graphical presentation and impactful combat all came together during my demo time to convince me Nintendo has something special in its hands that I can’t wait for you all to experience for yourselves.

extraction.body: The original The Legend of Zelda : Ocarina of Time has been certified as the highest-rated video game ever for a long time now. 2026’s Remake , however, has immediately climbed the charts and is currently this year’s top-rated title. The question then becomes, “Which one is actually better overall?” For my personal two cents, I still give the OG a slight edge. At the same time, that doesn’t take anything away from the Remake. In fact, 2026’s version of Ocarina is actually better in some cases. Let’s take a look at ten different ways Nintendo was able to take the classic and somehow improve on some aspects. Most obviously, the graphical and performance upgrades in OOT Remake are substantial. This isn’t a surprise at all since the OG is from the ’90s, but Remake still smashed it out of the park in terms of design and tone as well. Despite some concerns over glossy character models during the pre-launch phase of the game, the new art direction is constantly breathtaking and pulled off masterfully. Standouts are Lake Hylia with its gorgeous water effects, and Ganondorf’s Castle, which straight up looks like it’s ripped out of Mordor in Lord of the Rings. The hardest thing about going back for the original version of OOT is the control scheme and camera. Sure, the visuals are dated, but there’s a definite charm and style to them as well. The controls are just… old. This barrier to entry being removed in Zelda: Ocarina Remake was crucial to it succeeding in modern times. Thankfully, the right-stick camera works beautifully (though Z-Target centering was still kept in as well). Sword combat and shield blocking are fluid and snappy. Perhaps most importantly, however, is that projectile aiming can now be toggled between standard camera control and inverted. The 1998 game only offered inverted aiming, which is a total no-go for many modern gamers. There’s a certain charm in figuring out the auto-ledge jumping in N64 Ocarina, but it’s no surprise that having an actual, dedicated jump button in Remake is a massive improvement. Back in the day, Link’s jumping mechanics were the best Nintendo could muster, and we learned to adapt to them. But in 2026, not having an actual jump would’ve been a crime. This new ability also leads to some fun location and dungeon redesigns since Link can reach higher ledges and areas than ever before. A lot of players hopping into Remake (myself included) know almost everything about the N64 game. When picking up Remake, I wondered just how 1:1 everything would be, including things like gold skulltulas and room layouts. To my surprise, it was a blast to explore the new game and learn that many locations had been shuffled around or changed entirely. And this isn’t just a “better” change because it’s different. Instead, there are now several examples of things being placed more thoughtfully and satisfyingly in the game world. Take, for example, the Kokiri Sword, which now takes a little more parkour action to collect. I may know the lore and story of Zelda: Ocarina of Time better than any other video game. Upon recently replaying the OG, however, it’s funny how much of the narrative is a little bit underexplained. Case in point: the Triforce itself is shoddily explained, making it less impactful when considering why everyone seems to care so much about it. In Remake, most characters have a plethora of added or tweaked dialogue. A lot of this added exposition serves the game extremely well, making the stakes clearer and even giving us additional lore and info along the way. I didn’t expect to learn even more about Hyrule and the plot of the game in 2026, but the Remake gave me the opportunity. Growing up, we’d often have to make up video game character voices in our heads. Fully voice-acted games weren’t the norm yet. Aside from Navi shouting her classic “Hey!” and “Listen!” lines, the rest of the OG cast was relegated to grunts, screams, laughs, and moans. Hearing immediate narration voice-over when booting up Remake is a trip. For the most part, I found all the actor choices on-point, too. My personal standout is the English dub for Kaepora Gaebora, the Guiding Owl, played by Frank Todaro. There were doubts that Zelda: Ocarina of Time’s legendary soundtrack could be improved, but it somehow was. Of course, this is in large part due to the songs now being fully orchestrated, which was not an option on the Nintendo 64. Still, it wouldn’t have been hard to mess this one up with how beloved 1998’s tunes still are to this day. Thankfully, the full orchestration is gorgeous, as the new, sweeping melodies pack home way more emotion than ever before. Special shout-out to Saria’s Song, which comes back several times in a surprising, haunting fashion. While I wouldn’t say every dungeon was improved in the Remake, several were still fundamentally made better. In general, they’re all a bit more straightforward, which is nice for first-time players who aren’t used to retro game design. At the same time, simpler isn’t always better. In the case of dungeons like the Water Temple and Jabu-Jabu’s Belly, however, streamlining was the move. The migraine-inducing original Water Temple is reworked just enough that it went from my least favorite in the OG, to possibly my actual favorite in Remake. Most, if not all, of the dungeons are essentially at least on par with the original versions. The handful that actually made things better then stand out that much more this time around. While there aren’t too many challenging boss or enemy encounters in Zelda: Ocarina of Time Remake, fighting everything is still more fun than ever. passages: The original The Legend of Zelda : Ocarina of Time has been certified as the highest-rated video game ever for a long time now. 2026’s Remake , however, has immediately climbed the charts and is currently this year’s top-rated title. The question then becomes, “Which one is actually better overall?”
For my personal two cents, I still give the OG a slight edge. At the same time, that doesn’t take anything away from the Remake. In fact, 2026’s version of Ocarina is actually better in some cases.
Let’s take a look at ten different ways Nintendo was able to take the classic and somehow improve on some aspects.

Most obviously, the graphical and performance upgrades in OOT Remake are substantial. This isn’t a surprise at all since the OG is from the ’90s, but Remake still smashed it out of the park in terms of design and tone as well.
Despite some concerns over glossy character models during the pre-launch phase of the game, the new art direction is constantly breathtaking and pulled off masterfully.
Standouts are Lake Hylia with its gorgeous water effects, and Ganondorf’s Castle, which straight up looks like it’s ripped out of Mordor in Lord of the Rings.

The hardest thing about going back for the original version of OOT is the control scheme and camera. Sure, the visuals are dated, but there’s a definite charm and style to them as well. The controls are just… old.

This barrier to entry being removed in Zelda: Ocarina Remake was crucial to it succeeding in modern times. Thankfully, the right-stick camera works beautifully (though Z-Target centering was still kept in as well). Sword combat and shield blocking are fluid and snappy.

Perhaps most importantly, however, is that projectile aiming can now be toggled between standard camera control and inverted. The 1998 game only offered inverted aiming, which is a total no-go for many modern gamers.
There’s a certain charm in figuring out the auto-ledge jumping in N64 Ocarina, but it’s no surprise that having an actual, dedicated jump button in Remake is a massive improvement.
Back in the day, Link’s jumping mechanics were the best Nintendo could muster, and we learned to adapt to them. But in 2026, not having an actual jump would’ve been a crime.
This new ability also leads to some fun location and dungeon redesigns since Link can reach higher ledges and areas than ever before.

A lot of players hopping into Remake (myself included) know almost everything about the N64 game. When picking up Remake, I wondered just how 1:1 everything would be, including things like gold skulltulas and room layouts.
To my surprise, it was a blast to explore the new game and learn that many locations had been shuffled around or changed entirely. And this isn’t just a “better” change because it’s different.

Instead, there are now several examples of things being placed more thoughtfully and satisfyingly in the game world. Take, for example, the Kokiri Sword, which now takes a little more parkour action to collect.

I may know the lore and story of Zelda: Ocarina of Time better than any other video game. Upon recently replaying the OG, however, it’s funny how much of the narrative is a little bit underexplained. Case in point: the Triforce itself is shoddily explained, making it less impactful when considering why everyone seems to care so much about it.

In Remake, most characters have a plethora of added or tweaked dialogue. A lot of this added exposition serves the game extremely well, making the stakes clearer and even giving us additional lore and info along the way.
I didn’t expect to learn even more about Hyrule and the plot of the game in 2026, but the Remake gave me the opportunity.

Growing up, we’d often have to make up video game character voices in our heads. Fully voice-acted games weren’t the norm yet. Aside from Navi shouting her classic “Hey!” and “Listen!” lines, the rest of the OG cast was relegated to grunts, screams, laughs, and moans.

Hearing immediate narration voice-over when booting up Remake is a trip. For the most part, I found all the actor choices on-point, too. My personal standout is the English dub for Kaepora Gaebora, the Guiding Owl, played by Frank Todaro.

There were doubts that Zelda: Ocarina of Time’s legendary soundtrack could be improved, but it somehow was. Of course, this is in large part due to the songs now being fully orchestrated, which was not an option on the Nintendo 64.

Still, it wouldn’t have been hard to mess this one up with how beloved 1998’s tunes still are to this day. Thankfully, the full orchestration is gorgeous, as the new, sweeping melodies pack home way more emotion than ever before.
Special shout-out to Saria’s Song, which comes back several times in a surprising, haunting fashion.

While I wouldn’t say every dungeon was improved in the Remake, several were still fundamentally made better. In general, they’re all a bit more straightforward, which is nice for first-time players who aren’t used to retro game design. At the same time, simpler isn’t always better.

In the case of dungeons like the Water Temple and Jabu-Jabu’s Belly, however, streamlining was the move. The migraine-inducing original Water Temple is reworked just enough that it went from my least favorite in the OG, to possibly my actual favorite in Remake.
Most, if not all, of the dungeons are essentially at least on par with the original versions. The handful that actually made things better then stand out that much more this time around.

For example, King Dodongo now summons baby Dodongos during phases of the boss fight. Twinrova has an additional, arena-spanning spin attack. It’s a blast to have to reconsider and relearn these fights (and also practice them in the added Hall of Fallen Foes mode).

The best things here, however, are the standard enemy moveset tweaks. A lot of us have fought thousands of skulltulas, wolfos, and tektites. To see all these monsters throwing different moves out that are actively more fun to engage with is incredible.

Finally, OOT Remake does a wonderful job of making locations like Hyrule Castle Town and Kakariko Village feel more alive and lived-in than ever. Since time can pass in towns now, we’re treated to the game’s NPCs being on actual schedules and routines that we can follow and learn.

This makes everyone feel like that much more of a thought-out character in many cases. For example, Grog used to just sit under the tree in Kakariko at night in the N64 game, and we didn’t ever learn much about him.

Now, we can follow him around town, observing him lurking behind walls, waiting for his dad to go home so he doesn’t have to cross paths with him. It’s things like this that make Zelda: Ocarina of Time Remake feel more alive than ever.
