I’m not sure that price is worth it for the average user, but it’s not necessary to enjoy this well-rounded speaker.
Zoom is headed to Nest smart displays. / Google

Amazon may have introduced the smart display with the Echo Show , but Google refined the concept with its Nest Hub line, which reached its apex with the Nest Hub Max, a 10-inch smart display that also has strong sound. Again, Gemini for Home has notable improvements over Google Assistant, although it still has some work to do and more advanced AI subscriptions require higher monthly fees.

The Nest Hub Max will show you your spoken commands so you know Google heard you correctly, it can deftly walk you through a recipe from popular cooking websites and it works seamlessly with Google-supported smart home cameras and video doorbells to display their camera feeds onscreen. You can use it as a side browsing screen, a home control hub or anything else you need.
The best LED bulbs are smart, bright and ready for your home. / Tyler Lacoma/CNET

Smart bulbs come in many sizes, but almost all are made to fit the existing light sockets around your home. One of our favorites is this LED floodlight model from GE Cync, ideal for kitchens, entryways, living rooms and other big spaces with floodlights . Unlike other color smart bulbs, this GE Cync bulb has four quadrants that you can switch between any colors you want for an overlapping or complementary effect, giving your space whatever vibe you desire with just one bulb. It supports scheduling, voice commands and other smart bulb tricks that come in handy when you’re busy. We also found the GE Cync app particularly easy to use and really like that it has both Alexa and Google support. It’s the most complete smart light option we’ve found if you are looking for a floodlight.

At CNET we’re fans of how smart thermostats can save us money and make home temps easier to manage, but there are many choices and only room for one thermostat in your home. We love this Nest learning thermostat not only for its dazzling animations, but also for how it streamlines your savings with scheduling, eco modes and presence sensors that learn when your home is active and when it’s quiet.

You also get monthly reports tracking your energy use and showing you how to save. Even a pricey thermostat can pay for itself over a year or two with this kind of cost cutting — and your guests may just stop and stare at how pretty it looks. This particular model also comes with a satellite sensor to get temperature readings in especially hot or cold places to help control the thermostat more precisely.

The Arlo Pro 6 outdoor security camera is the latest upgrades to Arlo’s outdoor, wireless line of cameras. The design is better than ever, the 2K resolution is crystal clear, and the 160-degree field of view is enough to easily capture a whole yard or driveway. Arlo also offers strong smart home support and an option for an extended battery pack.

There’s one catch — Arlo’s cam requires a subscription to unlock video storage and its handy AI features, including the ability to recognize flames or provide event captions to summarize what happened when motion detection was activated. That costs at least $8 per month to activate, which means this camera is mostly for those who don’t mind a subscription. If you don’t like that, we have a guide on the best security cameras with no subscriptions , too.

If you’re a fan of Alexa and particularly the upgraded Alexa Plus conversational AI (free with an Amazon Prime subscription, otherwise $20), then this new 11-inch Echo Show could be the ideal hub for your smart home. It includes spatial audio upgrades and a larger screen that’s even better for catching up on streaming videos or TV shows while you’re working. Like Echo speakers, the display can answer questions, set reminders, make calls (video calls in this case) and control smart home technology. The upgraded Alexa Plus is also friendly and more capable than before, although you will need to connect your streaming services to get the most use out of this device. We like models like these for our kitchens and computer setups or similar areas.
Eufy's floodlight camera includes a particularly powerful cam. / Eufy

Most outdoor smart lights require an outdoor outlet, which limits placements. Govee’s option uses a solar panel to charge up the lights for a night’s performance. I’ve tried it in my backyard, and it really does work. Plus, Govee’s app offers dozens and dozens of different scenes to schedule or play with, from pulsing colors to gentle radiance in any hue you want. You can even ask an AI assistant to whip up a new color pattern or sync the lights to music.

The 33-foot string uses large durable bulbs made for outdoor spaces, but they will only cover a limited area. The good news is that you can put them anywhere as long as the panel gets some sunlight, including patios, porches, balconies, eaves and fences. To save battery life, you usually need to reconnect with Bluetooth when you want to change or update these lights.
Tiny devices such as a leak detector can make a world-changing difference in a home. / Tyler Lacoma/CNET
The Wyze Duo Pan Cam gives you more freedom over your security system than ever before.

Since this is a diverse group of products, there isn’t one set procedure we follow. (A test for a smart home display will tell you nothing about a mesh router.) Everything on this list (and the category-specific best lists) went through hands-on testing.

There are more commonalities, too. Where possible and relevant, we gather data in a standardized and empirical way. For testing Wi-Fi routers , that includes repeating the same speed test at a series of standard distances in the same house for each router that’s tested.

For other categories, the testing is more experiential. For devices like smart thermostats, smart speakers, smart plugs and smart home displays, we install and use them in the ways you would. When testing the second-gen Google Nest Hub , our reviewer conducted a two-week test of its sleep-tracking function in addition to its more obvious around-the-house capabilities.

Relevant company policies also factor into our reviews of these devices, especially when it comes to privacy concerns. Bringing a device into your home that can watch or listen to you or your neighbors comes with corresponding privacy concerns. CNET works to understand the company’s privacy policies, make them easy to understand and takes privacy questions directly to the companies like Ring and Google when the answers aren’t obvious.

Choosing the best smart home devices is a bit different than choosing headphones or a streaming service , since smart devices are often meant to be integrated into a smart home ecosystem. That means one of your first considerations should be compatibility. Consider devices that will work with the same voice assistant. CNET recommends both Google Assistant and Amazon’s Alexa as two of the best centerpieces for a smart home.

The other things to consider are your goals and your needs. Are you interested in connecting and automating as much of your house as possible? Then go all in on a connected home. If your problem is one person leaving their bedroom light on when they leave the house, a smart light bulb might do the trick.

Not to get all philosophical, but that depends on how you define worth. Smart home devices can add a layer of convenience to your life you’d be hard-pressed to achieve without them. Left a light on? Ask Google to turn it off. Need to add something to your grocery list? Tell Alexa.

Smart home devices can save you money, too. The best example of this is a smart thermostat, which can save you 10% on your energy bills if you program them right. Other devices like smart bulbs and smart plugs that you can schedule or shut off remotely can keep you from wasting energy when you’re away. Motion sensors connected to your lights can do the same trick.

Connecting smart devices at home is, generally relatively simple. Smart plugs, pet cams or smart light bulbs set up and connect easily. Even most devices with more involved installations, like smart thermostats, can be installed without too much fuss. (Although calling a professional is always a good idea if you’re unsure of yourself.)

If you’re looking for the best smart home hub and assistant, CNET has recognized Google Assistant and Amazon Alexa as two of the leading options. Both support thousands of devices, so you’re bound to find an option to fit your needs.

Greater connectivity among smart home devices is (likely) going to arrive soon. Matter, a project that aims to provide greater connectivity across smart home brands, is creeping closer to its debut. The frequently delayed effort has sign-on from some of the biggest smart home companies, although it’s always best to confirm a device you’re considering is compatible and not count on future developments.

Google, Amazon and Apple get the most attention for their smart home hubs and speakers, but plenty of other companies are making top-of-the-line products that can be incorporated into a smart home ecosystem.

CoreWeave’s financing strategy now revolves around those opportunities.
In August, the company closed a $2.6 billion loan, its first designed specifically for shorter-term customer contracts.
Known as DDTL 5.5, it lets CoreWeave borrow in installments as it needs the money.
CoreWeave is rewriting how it pays for the AI boom, according to the company’s third-quarter earnings , reported on Tuesday.

CoreWeave, a neocloud that rents out the computing power behind AI, said it’s increasingly asking customers to pay up front, borrowing against specific contracts, and even pursuing short-term deals that could lead to higher prices.

Instead, CoreWeave’s plan is to rely on loans backed by specific customer contracts, drawing on funds as needed to finance most of infrastructure it still has to build to deliver on its significant backlog of $132.5 billion.
Even though Wall Street reacted positively to CoreWeave’s earnings, bond investors are much less sanguine.
CoreWeave is also looking to capitalize on that growing demand by signing more shorter-term contracts that can command much higher prices.

The new strategies could help CoreWeave finance its growth more efficiently while squeezing more cash from existing infrastructure.
But these bets only hold if today’s demand and pricing power continue.
Lenders give more weight to longer-term contracts, even if they’re priced lower, because they value predictable cash flow and consistency to repay the loan above all.
In short, CoreWeave is finding new ways to expand without relying on unsecured debt.

Upfront payments could alleviate CoreWeave’s immediate borrowing needs, but they also commit the company to providing services at a price that might be less attractive down the road if compute demand continues to surge.
TechCrunch has reached out to CoreWeave for more information about its loan facility.

extraction.body: CoreWeave is rewriting how it pays for the AI boom, according to the company’s third-quarter earnings , reported on Tuesday. CoreWeave, a neocloud that rents out the computing power behind AI, said it’s increasingly asking customers to pay up front, borrowing against specific contracts, and even pursuing short-term deals that could lead to higher prices. The new strategies could help CoreWeave finance its growth more efficiently while squeezing more cash from existing infrastructure. But these bets only hold if today’s demand and pricing power continue. CoreWeave reported $3.66 billion in revenue, up 168% from the year prior, but it also posted a $709 million net loss and $846 million in quarterly interest expense. “We will not use the unsecured debt market to fund our business at current yields, nor do we need to,” CoreWeave CEO Michael Intrator said during Tuesday’s earnings call. Instead, CoreWeave’s plan is to rely on loans backed by specific customer contracts, drawing on funds as needed to finance most of infrastructure it still has to build to deliver on its significant backlog of $132.5 billion. CoreWeave also said it expects about $9 billion in customer prepayments and deposits over the next three months, including more than $3 billion tied to signing new customer contracts for capacity it has already built, which requires no additional spending on hardware. Rivals Nebius and IREN have also relied on hefty Microsoft prepayments to pay for computing capacity, signaling that the industry is moving toward asking Big Tech to pay up for their buildouts. Upfront payments could alleviate CoreWeave’s immediate borrowing needs, but they also commit the company to providing services at a price that might be less attractive down the road if compute demand continues to surge. CoreWeave is also looking to capitalize on that growing demand by signing more shorter-term contracts that can command much higher prices. The company raised prices across its offerings by about 25% in July and by another 10% later in the quarter. Prices are still climbing this quarter, in a way that “more than offset[s] cost increases,” said Intrator. “We are also allocating more capacity to short-term opportunities, where the pricing justifies it, selling capacity at more than $40 million per megawatt annually, while pricing for new infrastructure on four and five-year contracts is moving to $20 million to $25 million per megawatt,” the chief executive said. CoreWeave’s financing strategy now revolves around those opportunities. In August, the company closed a $2.6 billion loan, its first designed specifically for shorter-term customer contracts. Known as DDTL 5.5, it lets CoreWeave borrow in installments as it needs the money. While short-term deals let CoreWeave charge higher prices and change them more frequently, it’s a tradeoff. Lenders give more weight to longer-term contracts, even if they’re priced lower, because they value predictable cash flow and consistency to repay the loan above all. Even though Wall Street reacted positively to CoreWeave’s earnings, bond investors are much less sanguine. Last month, yields on some of the company’s bonds hit above 15%, highlighting that investors are concerned about the debt needed to fund data center buildouts before those investments see a return. In short, CoreWeave is finding new ways to expand without relying on unsecured debt. The strategy it has chosen could boost profits, but it also carries greater risk around contract renewals and pricing — and it just goes to show how dependent the AI infrastructure boom is on sustained, and as yet unproven, demand. TechCrunch has reached out to CoreWeave for more information about its loan facility. extraction.body: CoreWeave is rewriting how it pays for the AI boom, according to the company’s third-quarter earnings , reported on Tuesday. CoreWeave, a neocloud that rents out the computing power behind AI, said it’s increasingly asking customers to pay up front, borrowing against specific contracts, and even pursuing short-term deals that could lead to higher prices. The new strategies could help CoreWeave finance its growth more efficiently while squeezing more cash from existing infrastructure. But these bets only hold if today’s demand and pricing power continue. CoreWeave reported $3.66 billion in revenue, up 168% from the year prior, but it also posted a $709 million net loss and $846 million in quarterly interest expense. “We will not use the unsecured debt market to fund our business at current yields, nor do we need to,” CoreWeave CEO Michael Intrator said during Tuesday’s earnings call. Instead, CoreWeave’s plan is to rely on loans backed by specific customer contracts, drawing on funds as needed to finance most of infrastructure it still has to build to deliver on its significant backlog of $132.5 billion. CoreWeave also said it expects about $9 billion in customer prepayments and deposits over the next three months, including more than $3 billion tied to signing new customer contracts for capacity it has already built, which requires no additional spending on hardware. Rivals Nebius and IREN have also relied on hefty Microsoft prepayments to pay for computing capacity, signaling that the industry is moving toward asking Big Tech to pay up for their buildouts. Upfront payments could alleviate CoreWeave’s immediate borrowing needs, but they also commit the company to providing services at a price that might be less attractive down the road if compute demand continues to surge. CoreWeave is also looking to capitalize on that growing demand by signing more shorter-term contracts that can command much higher prices. The company raised prices across its offerings by about 25% in July and by another 10% later in the quarter. Prices are still climbing this quarter, in a way that “more than offset[s] cost increases,” said Intrator. “We are also allocating more capacity to short-term opportunities, where the pricing justifies it, selling capacity at more than $40 million per megawatt annually, while pricing for new infrastructure on four and five-year contracts is moving to $20 million to $25 million per megawatt,” the chief executive said. CoreWeave’s financing strategy now revolves around those opportunities. In August, the company closed a $2.6 billion loan, its first designed specifically for shorter-term customer contracts. Known as DDTL 5.5, it lets CoreWeave borrow in installments as it needs the money. While short-term deals let CoreWeave charge higher prices and change them more frequently, it’s a tradeoff. Lenders give more weight to longer-term contracts, even if they’re priced lower, because they value predictable cash flow and consistency to repay the loan above all. Even though Wall Street reacted positively to CoreWeave’s earnings, bond investors are much less sanguine. Last month, yields on some of the company’s bonds hit above 15%, highlighting that investors are concerned about the debt needed to fund data center buildouts before those investments see a return. In short, CoreWeave is finding new ways to expand without relying on unsecured debt. The strategy it has chosen could boost profits, but it also carries greater risk around contract renewals and pricing — and it just goes to show how dependent the AI infrastructure boom is on sustained, and as yet unproven, demand. TechCrunch has reached out to CoreWeave for more information about its loan facility. Axsome Therapeutics’ most important drug is performing well, and the company is well-positioned to expand its lineup over the medium term. On Thursday, Nov. 5, two days after the U.S. midterm elections, the tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite dropped by more than 5%, its worst single-day dip in over a year. The reason behind the sharp sell-off is no secret. Democrats emerged as the winners of the midterm elections, and now that they control both chambers of the U.S. Congress, investors are worried about what that means for artificial intelligence (AI) stocks. That's a reasonable worry, but even in this environment, there are attractive stocks worth buying and holding onto at least for the next five years. Here are two great examples to consider: Shopify (NASDAQ:SHOP) and Axsome Therapeutics (NASDAQ:AXSM) . Shopify is proving its resilience. Despite a challenging macroeconomic landscape and the threat AI poses to its business, the company's financial results have been pretty strong. In the third quarter, Shopify's revenue increased by 32% year over year to $3.7 billion, driven by a 29.5% increase in gross merchandise volume (GMV) to $119.1 billion. The company's gross profit jumped 28% year over year to $1.8 billion, while its net income, excluding the impact of equity investments, was $584 million, up 59% compared to the year-ago period. Shopify also posted free cash flow of $816 million at a 22% margin, versus $507 million in the third quarter of 2025 at an 18% margin. Management noted that AI-powered searches are helping boost the company's GMV and revenue. Shopify has built AI tools to help users find what they want more easily and to help merchants automate tasks and better reach customers. The results are showing up in the company's numbers. But we may still be in the early innings of this tailwind. AI has only just begun to change how people shop -- with agents aiding search and purchases -- and Shopify is positioning itself to capitalize on this as it becomes more common. Meanwhile, there remains a massive white space in the e-commerce industry . E-commerce transactions still account for fewer than one in five retail transactions in the U.S. Besides doubling down on AI tools, Shopify boasts a deep ecosystem of merchants whose feedback helps it improve its product offering. This grants the company a competitive edge through network effects. The stock is down 6% this year, but it has performed well since mid-May, and could beat the market over the next five years . Axsome Therapeutics is a biotech company focused on central nervous system diseases. The drugmaker has outperformed the broader market over the past five years and is well positioned to do so again. Axsome Therapeutics' portfolio of drugs includes Auvelity, currently its biggest growth driver, Sunosi, and Symbravo. The results of the recent U.S. midterm elections have rocked equity markets. Artificial intelligence (AI) stocks are being particularly affected, since voters overwhelmingly adopted measures that could lead to more restrictions on data center expansion. Let's consider three stocks that could be great buys following post-election dips: Apple ( AAPL +2.04% ) , Alphabet ( GOOG +2.00% ) ( GOOGL +2.11% ) , and Microsoft ( MSFT -2.26% ) . All three may still beat the market over the next five years. Here's why. Apple operates its own data centers to support its digital services. However, the company hasn't poured nearly as much money into data center construction as some of its similarly sized tech peers racing to meet the massive demand for AI services. What's more, Apple has outsourced some cloud computing workloads to third-party providers. In other words, the company is somewhat less exposed to the risk that increased regulatory scrutiny will lead to a slowdown in the construction of data centers than many of its peers. Apple has now recorded double-digit sales growth for four consecutive quarters, after spending a long time in single digits. AAPL Revenue (Quarterly YoY Growth) data by YCharts Apple could continue to perform well over the next year or two, especially as the recently launched iPhone Duo, the company's first foldable smartphone, has been a hit so far. Over the long run, expect Apple to continue expanding its installed base, growing its subscription revenue, and posting consistent revenue and earnings growth. The company is pouring significant sums into its AI-related ambitions, so much so that its free cash flow has turned negative in the past two quarters. True, cloud and AI have been performing the best in recent quarters, but Alphabet still generates most of its revenue from its advertising business, thanks to its Google search engine and YouTube video-sharing platform, both of which are among the undisputed leaders in these markets. Microsoft is well positioned to benefit if the AI industry continues to expand without a hitch, but it is also well equipped to navigate the various headwinds it might encounter. And continued demand for its legacy services could help drive sales and earnings higher either way. extraction.body: Equity markets are experiencing significant volatility following the midterm elections, but investors should look beyond that. The results of the recent U.S. midterm elections have rocked equity markets. Artificial intelligence (AI) stocks are being particularly affected, since voters overwhelmingly adopted measures that could lead to more restrictions on data center expansion. That's bad news for many AI leaders, but despite this setback, my view is that the AI industry will continue to expand over the long run. Let's consider three stocks that could be great buys following post-election dips: Apple ( AAPL +2.04% ) , Alphabet ( GOOG +2.00% ) ( GOOGL +2.11% ) , and Microsoft ( MSFT -2.26% ) . All three may still beat the market over the next five years. Here's why. Apple operates its own data centers to support its digital services. However, the company hasn't poured nearly as much money into data center construction as some of its similarly sized tech peers racing to meet the massive demand for AI services. What's more, Apple has outsourced some cloud computing workloads to third-party providers. In other words, the company is somewhat less exposed to the risk that increased regulatory scrutiny will lead to a slowdown in the construction of data centers than many of its peers. Meanwhile, the company's financial results remain pretty strong, as the latest iPhone continues to drive a strong renewal cycle. During Apple's fourth quarter of 2026, for the period ended Sept. 26, Apple reported $114.5 billion in sales, up 12% year over year. Apple has now recorded double-digit sales growth for four consecutive quarters, after spending a long time in single digits. AAPL Revenue (Quarterly YoY Growth) data by YCharts Apple could continue to perform well over the next year or two, especially as the recently launched iPhone Duo, the company's first foldable smartphone, has been a hit so far. Over the long run, expect Apple to continue expanding its installed base, growing its subscription revenue, and posting consistent revenue and earnings growth. The regulatory impact of the midterm elections could weigh on Alphabet, one of the biggest hyperscalers. The company is pouring significant sums into its AI-related ambitions, so much so that its free cash flow has turned negative in the past two quarters. The tech leader's plans may have to be scaled back if lawmakers crack down on data center expansion. However, there are several reasons why Alphabet could perform well regardless. Let's discuss three. First, the company has a diversified business. True, cloud and AI have been performing the best in recent quarters, but Alphabet still generates most of its revenue from its advertising business, thanks to its Google search engine and YouTube video-sharing platform, both of which are among the undisputed leaders in these markets. Second, if there is a halt, or at least a slowdown, in data center construction while demand for the compute capacity new facilities could provide remains strong, it could mean increased pricing power and margins for owners of existing capacity. And few corporations have more available capacity than Alphabet. Of course, the increased demand and higher prices for existing capacity might not be enough to offset the losses from being unable to expand. But the point is, Alphabet is in a much better position to navigate the uncertainty ahead than it appears at first. And the company's outlook over the next five years remains attractive as it taps into multiple fast-growing industries. Microsoft is in a similar boat. It is one of the biggest hyperscalers and may experience increased demand for existing compute capacity over the next couple of years if regulators impose increased restrictions on the AI industry's expansion plans. Microsoft is also a fairly diversified company that generates significant revenue from long-term contracts with millions of clients that rely on its software services in their day-to-day activities. The company had $677 billion in commercial remaining performance obligations as of Sept. 30, up 73% year over year. Microsoft expects to recognize about 30% of that in the next 12 months. Microsoft is well positioned to benefit if the AI industry continues to expand without a hitch, but it is also well equipped to navigate the various headwinds it might encounter. And continued demand for its legacy services could help drive sales and earnings higher either way. Finally, Microsoft is an excellent dividend stock compared to most of its similarly-sized tech peers. Reinvesting the dividend will help boost returns over the next five years. passages: Cryptocurrencies recovered some of Tuesday's losses as institutional developments and easing selling pressure offered encouraging signs.

Cryptocurrency markets rebounded on Wednesday, November 11, recovering some of the previous session's losses as selling pressure eased and new institutional disclosures highlighted growing Wall Street exposure to digital assets. As of early evening, Bitcoin ( BTC +0.14% ) climbed 1.24% to $74,621.63, while Ethereum ( ETH +0.21% ) gained 1.30% to $2,077.30 and Solana ( SOL -0.26% ) advanced 1.94% to $84.87.

The recovery comes despite persistent inflation concerns and uncertainty surrounding Federal Reserve monetary policy, suggesting investors remain cautiously optimistic about the cryptocurrency market's longer-term outlook.

Bitcoin showed signs of stabilization on Wednesday as selling pressure from U.S. spot Bitcoin ETFs began to ease. The slowdown in outflows offered some relief after several sessions of sustained selling.

Meanwhile, new regulatory filings revealed growing exposure to Bitcoin ETFs among major Wall Street banks. Barclays ( BCS +0.22% ) increased its holdings in BlackRock's iShares Bitcoin Trust ETF ( IBIT +1.34% ) by 48% during the third quarter, bringing its position to approximately $187 million. Citigroup ( C +1.59% ) also disclosed a new $119 million position in Fidelity's Bitcoin ETF while increasing its BlackRock holdings by roughly 50%.

The disclosures point to growing institutional participation in regulated cryptocurrency products, even as near-term market conditions remain challenging. However, the filings reflect holdings as of September 30, rather than fresh buying during November's sell-off, making current ETF flows a more timely indicator of investor demand.
iShares Bitcoin Trust ETF rose 1.34%, Fidelity Wise Origin Bitcoin Fund ( FBTC +1.30% ) rose 1.30%, and iShares Ethereum Trust ETF ( ETHA +1.23% ) rose 1.23%.

Wednesday's rebound offered some relief for cryptocurrency investors, but the broader market remains under pressure following five consecutive weeks of declines in Bitcoin. While signs of stabilizing institutional flows are encouraging, a single positive session does little to reverse the recent deterioration in market momentum.

For Bitcoin, reclaiming $76,000 will be an important first step toward restoring its short-term market structure and establishing a more sustainable recovery. Failure to recover that level could leave the cryptocurrency vulnerable to further selling, particularly if ETF outflows accelerate or macroeconomic conditions deteriorate.

Ethereum faces a similar test, with $2,000 emerging as a critical support level. Holding above that threshold could help stabilize sentiment, while a sustained break lower would increase downside risks. Solana, meanwhile, needs to reclaim approximately $98 to signal a more meaningful recovery from its recent decline.
The coming weeks will be crucial in determining whether Wednesday's gains mark the beginning of a broader recovery or merely a temporary rebound.

passages: Long-term forecasts still point to Bitcoin (CRYPTO:BTC) reaching hundreds of thousands of dollars by 2030, while projections for Ethereum (CRYPTO:ETH) vary from losses to gains of nearly five times its current value.
Five years from now is late 2031, so here's what Bitcoin and Ethereum could be worth in 5 years.
Yahoo Finance is not a broker-dealer or investment adviser and does not offer securities or cryptocurrencies for sale or facilitate trading.
As of November 10, U.S. spot Bitcoin ETFs, which hold Bitcoin and trade like stocks, held $92.8 billion in net assets.

Their cumulative net inflows, total money added minus withdrawals, fell to $55.4 billion from $57.96 billion on October 21, after outflows of $430.2 million on November 5 and $411.9 million on November 6.
Ethereum's 56.2% drop over the past five years, against Bitcoin's 14.9% gain, suggests the lower end of projections isn't far-fetched.

If Bitcoin falls below its June 30 low of $58,566, about 21% lower, or Ethereum drops below its June 25 low of $1,566, about 24% lower, the bear numbers in both tables could become the likelier five-year outcome.
That fits the pattern of Ethereum falling harder than Bitcoin during market sell-offs.

Bitcoin has an edge from its fixed supply and deeper ETF base, while Ethereum offers staking rewards and more upside per dollar if network fees recover, a trade-off weighed in our look at the better hold through 2027.

Long-term forecasts still point to Bitcoin ( CRYPTO:BTC ) reaching hundreds of thousands of dollars by 2030, while projections for Ethereum ( CRYPTO:ETH ) vary from losses to gains of nearly five times its current value. Five years from now is late 2031, so here’s what Bitcoin and Ethereum could be worth in 5 years.
Bitcoin trades at $73,899, down 41.4% from its all-time high of $126,080 on October 6, 2025. Ethereum trades at $2,054, down 58.5% from its high of $4,946 on August 24, 2025.

Both cryptocurrencies have declined over the past month, and Ethereum has fallen more sharply. Bitcoin has fallen 9.5% over 30 days, from $84,082 on October 21 to $73,721 on November 10, while Ethereum is down 16% over the same stretch. That fits the pattern of Ethereum falling harder than Bitcoin during market sell-offs.
Few analysts publish 2031 price targets, so the tables below use 2030 projections where 2031 figures are unavailable.

Bitcoin would need to rise 125% to reach the lowest projection and 71% to reclaim its all-time high. ARK’s $710,000 base forecast would put Bitcoin’s market value at about $14.27 trillion with the current supply of around 20.1 million coins, compared to a market cap of roughly $1.49 trillion today. With supply capped at 21 million, new coins barely change that math.

Ethereum has no maximum supply, making it harder to reach previous highs. About 122.2 million ETH are in circulation, up from about 120.7 million in October 2025. To return to the $4,946 high, Ethereum would need a market value near $604.4 billion, up from a current market cap of around $251 billion, requiring a 141% rise to recover that peak.

If Ethereum hits $10,000 in the bull scenario, its market cap would reach $1.22 trillion, a size it has never reached, after a 387% increase. On the downside, the $1,500 bear scenario means a 27% drop, so a $1,000 Ethereum stake by 2030 could end in either a loss or a significant gain.

As of November 10, U.S. spot Bitcoin ETFs , which hold Bitcoin and trade like stocks, held $92.8 billion in net assets. Their cumulative net inflows, total money added minus withdrawals, fell to $55.4 billion from $57.96 billion on October 21, after outflows of $430.2 million on November 5 and $411.9 million on November 6.

ETF buying has driven Bitcoin’s price before. After the funds launched, Bitcoin rose from about $42,611 at the end of January 2024 to $73,628 by March 2024. Corporate treasuries add a second buyer, led by Strategy Inc. ( NASDAQ:MSTR ), which owns 850,364 BTC, roughly 4.2% of circulating supply, according to its November 9 filing.

U.S. spot Ethereum ETFs held $12.1 billion on November 9, and their cumulative inflows dropped to $11.74 billion on November 10, from $13.2 billion on October 13. Demand for Ethereum ETFs has boosted its price before, pushing it from $1,383 in April 2025 to an all-time high in August 2025.

Staking, where holders lock their ETH to secure the network in exchange for rewards, reached an all-time high of 43.8 million ETH in October, according to Bitwise data. However, Token Terminal data shows that stablecoins and funds on the Ethereum network fell 19% to $168.3 billion after the KelpDAO exploit, and less money on the network means fewer fees burned.

Forecasts for 2030 range from ARK’s $300,000 bear scenario to its $1.2 million bull scenario. A more realistic expectation by 2031 falls in the low-to-mid six figures, in line with our end-of-decade math for one Bitcoin .

The 2030 scenarios for Ethereum range from $1,500 to $10,000. Reaching the $5,000 base target, 143% above its current price, would rely on stronger ETF inflows and recovering network fees. Ethereum’s 56.2% drop over the past five years, against Bitcoin’s 14.9% gain, suggests the lower end of projections isn’t far-fetched.

The choice depends on an investor’s comfort with price swings. Bitcoin has an edge from its fixed supply and deeper ETF base, while Ethereum offers staking rewards and more upside per dollar if network fees recover, a trade-off weighed in our look at the better hold through 2027 .

Bitcoin could reach the low-to-mid six figures by late 2031 if it regains $126,080 by the end of 2027, while Ethereum could end up near $5,000, with $10,000 less likely. Ethereum has the wider range of outcomes because its supply keeps growing, its ETF base is much smaller, and its value is tied to a fee recovery that hasn’t begun.

To regain their all-time highs , both coins need ETF cumulative inflows to climb back above their October peaks of $57.96 billion for Bitcoin and $13.2 billion for Ethereum. If Bitcoin falls below its June 30 low of $58,566, about 21% lower, or Ethereum drops below its June 25 low of $1,566, about 24% lower, the bear numbers in both tables could become the likelier five-year outcome.

If you are experiencing domestic violence or know someone who may be experiencing abuse, we encourage you to reach out for help and explore the resources listed below," West Linn police wrote in a post on its Facebook page.
In posts online, including the Facebook group "Are We Dating the Same Guy?," the women reported the abusive and coercive behavior, investigators said.
